title: IMB missionaries use home, cafes, apps to open doors for gospel conversations in Spain
summary: Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise w
content: Men and women gather to discuss spiritual topics with Caleb and Carina Beaty, International Mission Board missionaries who serve in Madrid. IMB Photo Across Spain, people looking for connection and meaningful conversation turn to the internet to find groups where they can meet others. At a café by the river, Caleb and Carina Beaty engage in conversations about finding purpose, beauty and “what’s wrong with the world.” A website called Meetup allows people to search for groups to meet in person. The description of the Beatys’ group indicates that it discusses spiritual topics. People come expecting to talk about faith, so it’s not a surprise when they arrive. Caleb said he always has a list of questions that begin broadly and funnel into questions such as, “If there were a God …” or “What do you think Christians believe about that?” or “Why do you think religions have such different perspectives?” The Beatys’ goal in these conversations is to work toward deeper worldview questions within 45 minutes to an hour. Most of the people who attend their Meetup group are from Madrid, but they also have conversations with people from other countries. During one Meetup, Caleb and Carina shared how creation was perfect, but sin led to a world separated from the Father. God offers salvation through the death and resurrection of Jesus, they explained. “There are times we’re able to get to a clear gospel presentation with a group of people, and sometimes we’re doing pre-evangelism.” Caleb said. Some repeat attendees who have been attending for more than a year quickly jump to the heart of the discussion. “All right, Caleb, what’s the Bible say about suffering?” they’ll ask. Caleb and Carina then have the opportunity to share the Christian perspective. IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty and their children pose for a photo in a park in Madrid, Spain.  IMB Photo Spain has secularized rapidly since the 1990s, Caleb said. While many may think of it as a Catholic nation, many people do not know the basic tenets of Christianity. “We’ve got all the churches, we’ve got the cathedrals, and they do processions, but the average person on the street does not know anything about the gospel and does not know anything about Jesus,” Caleb said. Younger Spaniards are drawn to their group and are receptive to the gospel because they don’t have a spiritual foundation or know anyone who does. “There’s just this curiosity because, for a lot of them, they’ve never met someone who actually believes that God exists, and that changes your life,” Carina said. “I’ve had people completely shocked that we believe in God. ‘You really believe that God exists?’ They can’t wrap their mind around that.” During one Meetup, a man contrasted Protestant and Catholic beliefs by saying Protestants focus on Jesus’ suffering and Catholics on Mary’s grief. Caleb responded that evangelicals focus on the resurrection. When Caleb said Jesus rose from the dead, the man replied that he needed to look into that. Caleb said encounters like that reveal how little many Spaniards know about the gospel. Caleb noted the irony of the man’s sharing the Catholic perspective without truly understanding it. He is not the only person the Beatys have met who has missed the heart of the gospel. A friend of the Beatys told them she’d heard Jesus died, but she hadn’t heard he rose from the dead. A man reads a passage of Scripture during a Bible study hosted by IMB missionaries Caleb and Carina Beaty at their family’s apartment in Madrid, Spain. Five atheists began attending their Bible study after attending the couple’s Meetup group. IMB Photo The Beatys also host seasonal outreach events through the Meetup. Members from their church in Madrid have started attending the Meetup to learn how the Beatys lead discussions. Their group has become so popular, a waitlist has formed. Caleb and Carina host a small-group Bible study in their home. Five atheists who joined their Meetup now attend the Bible study.
author: Tessa Sanchez

title: AAEO, LMCO totals signal Southern Baptist support for, focus on Great Commission

The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion
content: IMB Graphic NASHVILLE – As the books closed on the latest fiscal year, receipts for the two Southern Baptist national annual missions offerings underscored the value Southern Baptist churches place on reaching the world with the gospel. The Lottie Moon Christmas Offering® (LMCO) totaled $212.5 million to support International Mission Board (IMB) missionaries, and the Annie Armstrong Easter Offering® (AAEO) reached $73.6 million to support the North American Mission Board’s (NAMB) church planting, compassion ministry and other evangelistic efforts to reach North America. IMB President Paul Chitwood said he celebrates what God did in the 2025-26 season and what He is doing now to lead Southern Baptists toward historic generosity. “I thank God for Southern Baptists! With giving through the Lottie Moon offering at an all-time high, churches and individual givers continue to display a heart for the gospel to be proclaimed to every nation, all tribes, peoples and languages,” Chitwood said. The Annie total marked the second highest in NAMB’s history. The record Lottie Moon offering total surpassed last year’s total by more than $5 million and is the best offering in IMB history. “God is giving our generation unprecedented opportunity to send missionaries to the most unreached peoples and places,” Chitwood continued. “Though the challenges faced by our missionaries are enormous, the generosity of Southern Baptists ensures they have what they need to face those challenges and continue in the work while we hold the ropes with our support.” IMB missionary Landon Williams (center) walks with a Chilean pastor and a U.S. pastor on a remote island in Chile. Cooperation and generosity among Southern Baptists fuels the work to reach the uttermost parts of the world with the gospel. IMB Photo National goals for both offerings are set in partnership with Woman’s Missionary Union (WMU) each year. In response to the offering totals, Sandy Wisdom-Martin, executive director-treasurer of WMU, said: “As Southern Baptists, we are all in for His mission. When we give sacrificially, we prioritize the mission of God. Together our fervent prayers, our faithful generosity and our wholehearted obedience become channels for the gospel to reach our neighbors as well as the nations.” For the last 10 years, Southern Baptists have increasingly supported the Annie offering, setting records in seven of the last 10 years. Totals in each of the last four years have surpassed $70 million. “I am so grateful to the pastors and churches for the faithfulness and generosity they have demonstrated through this offering,” said NAMB president Kevin Ezell. “As I travel and speak in churches of all sizes, I love seeing the posters in the hallways showing their offering goals. For some it is a few hundred dollars, for others several thousand.” The Annie Armstrong offering supports more than 3,000 missionaries in North America, including the ongoing work of church planting in the U.S. and Canada. In 2025, Southern Baptists planted the largest number of churches, 699, since 2016. Including church plants and replants, Southern Baptists have surpassed 700 new churches in four of the last five years. More than 12,000 churches have been planted since 2010. To go along with the increased giving totals to the SBC’s missions offerings, Southern Baptists have also increased their local outreach efforts, indicating that the focus is not just on giving but on sending. Baptism totals have increased in each of the last five years, recovering from the pandemic-year low in 2020 to surpass the 2017 total. The five consecutive years of increase marked the first such streak in approximately 75 years. To Jordan Adams, unheard of things like 38 baptisms in one worship service have become “heard of” for his congregation. Several years ago, Adams planted a church in West Lafayette, Indiana, to reach students at Purdue University. “Now,” he says, “we’re seeing a movement of the gospel that I’m convince

title: A Maker’s Heart
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Holly Neal turned a lifelong love of creating into an unexpected opportunity to support sign language Bible translation.   The post  A Maker’s Heart  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Holly Neal loves people, and she loves making things. And when something catches her interest, she dives in. “I’m a maker,” she said simply. But making has become more than just a hobby for Holly. Through some of her family’s hardest seasons, it has offered them comfort and connection. And eventually it became an unexpected way to give back to what God is doing around the world. When Holly’s adult daughter Julia was being treated for leukemia, a friend invited them to learn how to quilt. The creative process gave Holly something to focus on as their family walked through a difficult season. It became a way to work through hard things alongside her daughter. Years later, when Holly’s grandson Graham was born during the COVID-19 pandemic, she reached for another familiar project: cross-stitching. Graham spent his first four months in the hospital. And because of visitation restrictions at the time, Holly spent long hours waiting in the cafeteria. So she brought her cross-stitch. Being busy helped calm Holly’s mind. Cross-stitching was a small, practical way to make the waiting a little easier. Holly and her husband, Steve, have continued to navigate some unique family circumstances as they’ve cared for their daughter and grandson. So when Chris and Lindsay Beals, Holly and Steven’s daughter and son-in-law, invited the couple to a Wycliffe event, they were especially excited. After a season of isolation, they looked forward to reconnecting with other Christians and hearing stories about what God was doing through Bible translation. One part of the work specifically stayed with Holly: sign language Bible translation. Curious about what sign language Bible translation actually looks like? See for yourself when you visit our interactive Bible Translation Experience! You’ll go on a global journey where you’ll meet some of the hardworking Deaf translators bringing the Bible to their people in a language and format that capture their hearts. Start your journey! → As a grandmother of a child with unique needs, Holly has a special place in her heart for communities and families who navigate specific challenges and contexts. Learning about the work of making God’s Word accessible to Deaf communities worldwide gave Holly a personal connection to a ministry she’d never fully understood before. Holly and Steve had already talked and prayed about a financial gift they wanted to make to Wycliffe. But as she continued thinking about the ministry and Bible translation projects for sign languages, another question kept coming to mind: “Steve and I had already come up with a number that we felt like to donate, but the Lord kept speaking to me. And I kept thinking, ‘But what can I do? … That’s our money, but how can I make an impact?’” So Holly began thinking about how much she had invested — in supplies, patterns, fabric and tools — over the years in her love of crafting. She wondered if some of those things could become part of her gift to Bible translation. And what if Holly passed some of those supplies along to other makers and used the proceeds to support Bible translation for sign languages? See how one couple in Alabama also creatively used their gifts and skills to give back to Bible translation → Giving in Community Holly decided to hold what the stitching community calls a “destash” — an opportunity for her to sell supplies she already owned to other stitchers who could put them to good use. She shared the idea through her YouTube channel and social media, where she had already connected with a community of people who love cross-stitch. So when Holly told her stitching community about Wycliffe and her desire to support sign language Bible translation, she invited them into partnering with something that mattered to her. And people responded with generosity! Some people paid more for supplies and projects than the asking price, wanting to give a little extra toward the cause. One woman Holly had never met was especially moved by the oppor

title: Discipling Your Child’s Heart (A Chat with Melissa Paredes)
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Your church can help bring God’s Word to people still waiting. Wycliffe’s Scott Ross shares how prayer, service and initiatives like Adopt a Verse connect local congregations with Bible translation around the world.   The post  Discipling Your Child’s Heart (A Chat with Melissa Paredes)  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . While the change in numbers is exciting, what’s more important is what they signify: Every number represents a person who has a story that matters to God. For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. That statement bears repeating: There will now be people who never remember a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. From the first word of Genesis to the last word of Revelation, the Bible tells one incredible story: God’s love for the world and His invitation for people from every nation and language to know Him. Get a glimpse of how God continues writing this story today as more and more people are experiencing the power of His Word. Watch the video → A New Generation Growing Up With God’s Word Let’s take a look at some of the recent communities that are experiencing not only life transformation but generational transformation as they encounter Jesus personally through Scripture. Jakalteko | Guatemala The Jakalteko Bible was dedicated in July 2026 in Guatemala! During the celebration, John 1:1-18 was read aloud — a passage that focuses on Christ, the eternal Word and our Redeemer. Early on, many women in the community memorized Job 19 . Like Job, they had faced various hardships in their lives and identified with his suffering. The book reminded them that God remains in control and that, in the midst of difficult circumstances, their Redeemer will deliver them and comfort them in their pain. Today, they have the full counsel of God’s Word and can now see this Redeemer fulfilled in Jesus in the New Testament. They are overjoyed that the Bible has arrived in the language they were born into! When the Bible was distributed, one mother who is raising her family alone said with joy and tears: “Thank God we have the Bible in our language. Now

title: Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Ken and Sally discovered a way to give God’s Word — a gift they’d had access to their whole lives — to others.    The post  Living Out a Legacy of Stewardship and Faith  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: What did your journey to faith look like? Perhaps it was a story of how God showed up in the midst of uncertainty, doubt or fears. Maybe it involved Him seeking you out and rescuing you. Or maybe you grew up in a Christian household and your story is a bit different — perhaps your family regularly read the Bible together and have always known about Jesus’ love. Ken Trager was raised that way. He reflected, “I think when you’re raised in a Christian home … and you have the routines of a life that is built around church and prayer, you just take it for granted.” He added, “It was just the air I breathed.” For Ken and his wife, Sally, faith was always part of their stories. They were each raised in Christian homes, followed Christ, got baptized and had parents who faithfully modeled church attendance, prayer and generosity.  Ken and Sally’s paths eventually crossed at Greenville University in southern Illinois, where they met and fell in love. They went on to build a life centered around family, faith and service. Ken spent his career as a teacher and coach while Sally worked as an accountant, and together they raised two children. Now retired, they’ve moved to be closer to their children and grandchildren, giving them a new opportunity to pour into the next generation. Through all those years and seasons, the faith Ken and Sally had seen modeled by their families continued to shape their home. Early in their marriage, Ken and Sally met a mentor who encouraged the couple to go deeper with their faith — to study Scripture, ask questions and wrestle honestly with what they believed. It was an important season of discovering that the faith that had been passed down from their families could also become something they personally owned and lived out together. What Do You Take for Granted? Years later, the couple experienced an aha moment when they were introduced to Wycliffe at an event. There, Ken and Sally heard story after story from people who had received Scripture in their own languages. Something clicked for Sally: “We’ve never known a day where we couldn’t access the Bible. And these people have just longed for it, and they’re finally getting it.” For the first time, something that had always surrounded the couple became visible — and it was a gift they could no longer take for granted . Ken and Sally had spent years thinking about the importance of God’s Word. Seeing people receive Scripture in their own languages helped them understand just how extraordinary that access is. “The power of salvation comes through that,” Ken said. “I can’t think of … [a more] important work than providing God’s Word to everybody in the world.” Sally agreed. “To have His Word is as if we’re hearing the voice of God,” she said. “God works through His Word.” This conviction — for people around the world to be able to access Scripture for themselves — became one of the reasons Ken and Sally prioritized a place in their giving for Wycliffe. But it also became part of a larger question about generosity they had been asking themselves for years: “If everything we have is a gift from God, what does it look like to live generously with it?” A Generous Heart Generosity, like faith, was something Ken and Sally had grown up around. Ken remembers his dad giving him money to put in the offering plate, and Sally remembers watching her parents give not just to their church but to people and organizations in need. Sally’s father especially enjoyed giving anonymously. As Ken and Sally have grown older, they’ve learned that generosity isn’t simply about giving a certain percentage or checking a box; it’s about continually asking what it means to have a generous heart . content: How old were you when you first learned that Jesus loves you? Perhaps you’ve always known it and can’t remember a day when you didn’t know the song “Jesus Loves Me” or couldn’t recite John 3:16 by heart. Maybe you were a teenager and learned about Jesus’ love through a friend or church summer camp. Or were in college and went to a concert where the gospel was clearly articulated. Maybe you were in the trenches of the workforce, and a coworker boldly shared with you about the God who radically changed their life. Regardless of how old you were, each of us who has chosen to follow Jesus has an origin story — a moment in our lives when the knowledge that “Jesus loves me, this I know, for the Bible tells me so” moved from head knowledge to heart belief. And from then on, our lives were transformed forever. This is the truth of the gospel and the power of understanding that Jesus loves you. People around the world are discovering the personal truth of John 3:16 for themselves in a language and format they clearly understand. Explore why understanding that “God so loved the world” transforms entire communities → A Changing Reality Throughout Christian history, the gospel has spread from one community to the next. Stories were told and retold, Scripture was translated, churches were planted, and discipleship deepened as people learned more about Jesus. Bible translation is foundational to all ministries of the church. It fuels evangelism, church planting, discipleship and more. It equips people to move from a blurry picture of who God is to a clear understanding and personal encounter with Jesus as Lord. Through Scripture, people are able to read, hear or see the love of God on display. Just two decades ago, most of the world’s language communities still needed Bible translation work to begin , let alone be completed. But praise God, in the last few years, we’ve seen tremendous progress made, with Bible translation underway in more languages than ever before . For these communities, the stories of future generations are being completely rewritten as children will now grow up never remembering a day when they didn’t have access to God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. title: 5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Prayer is essential to Bible translation. Explore five specific ways to pray for local churches, translation teams and communities around the world.   The post  5 Ways to Pray for Bible Translation Around the World  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Before His ascension to heaven, Jesus called the whole Church to “go and make disciples of all the nations” ( Matthew 28:18, NLT ), a command often referred to now as the Great Commission. God’s plan was to build His Kingdom in and through the Church, including local churches in every corner of the globe. And that’s exactly what’s happening today! God is on the move, and His Spirit is being poured out upon the earth in ways we’ve never seen before, particularly in the history of Bible translation. For so long, the Church was viewed as having the deepest roots and strongest influence in the West, with the West sending out Bible translators to the farthest reaches of the world. But over the last half century, the Church has exploded, expanding South and East and shifting the landscape of Bible translation with it. Johnstone Ndunde, executive director of SIL Global, a key partner of Wycliffe’s, shared: “In the world where we serve, we have many churches that have discipled, educated people [who] are able to serve the Lord as well. God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” “God’s mission is no longer from the West to the rest. It is from everyone to everywhere.” This is God’s hand at work. He desires for people from every language and community to experience His redemptive power through the blood of Jesus, leading to life transformation. Scripture in a language and format they clearly understand plays a vital role in that, enabling them to know God more deeply and grow through discipleship. Today, as the Great Commission is being advanced by the global Church, local churches are taking ownership and linking arms with Wycliffe and other Bible translation agencies around the world to ensure that their communities, countries and even entire regions have God’s Word. Prayer is foundational to seeing God’s Word translated and made accessible to every person still waiting. Whether you’re praying for local churches, translation teams or communities, your prayers matter. Here are five ways you can pray for Bible translation today: Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships Pray for Wisdom and Strength for Bible Translation Teams Pray for Deaf Communities to Encounter Jesus Through Sign Language Pray for More People to Join the Work of Bible Translation Pray for the Translation of the Full Bible 1. Pray for Local Churches and Bible Translation Partnerships As a result of missions and technology, the gospel has spread to more communities than ever before, and now local churches worldwide are rising up to establish evangelism, discipleship, church planting and other activities in their own communities — with Bible translation central to all of those efforts! As local churches work with Bible translation organizations to translate Scripture for their own communities, that partnership is accelerating the pace of the work. This shift to local church ownership is a direct answer to decades of faithful prayer and service. Praise God! PRAY WITH US Heavenly Father, Thank You for how You are raising up men and women who not only love You but who want to be part of sharing the gospel in their own communities, countries and regions. Your love is capturing more people as they encounter You personally in a language and format they clearly understand. Equip local churches to spread Your light and love to their families and neighbors, drawing people to You through Scripture. Amen. Your Prayers Keep Us Going | The Philippines Divine Grace Leparto, a Bible translation field coordinator in the Philippines, shares the story of a translator who returned home from a weeklong Bible translation workshop to find that much of her land had been seized while she was away. Despite this difficult loss, she continued serving in Bible translation, grateful for the ways she could see the Lord at work in her community. Her experience is just one example of the challenges translation team members can face as the

title: Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: Rediscover the wonder of Christmas by focusing on God’s faithfulness and the hope found in Jesus.   The post  Finding Wonder in the Midst of Christmas Weariness  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Christmas is supposed to be a season of wonder. Twinkling lights, familiar songs, meaningful traditions and time with people you love can all point toward the joy of celebrating Jesus’ birth. But when your December calendar fills with responsibilities and expectations, weariness can settle in before you realize it. Maybe you remember a time when Christmas felt different. As a child, you may have counted down the days and experienced joy in even the smallest traditions. As an adult, you might find yourself simply trying to catch your breath as you move from one responsibility to the next. In the middle of trying to make Christmas special for everyone else, it can be easy to miss the wonder yourself. But the Christmas story gives you an opportunity to slow down and remember what this season is really about. In Luke 1, before the story of Jesus’ birth begins, you meet people who knew what it meant to wait, wonder and trust that God was at work even when they couldn’t yet see what He was doing. Weary of Waiting Luke’s account of the life of Jesus doesn’t begin with Jesus’ birth; it begins instead with the story of Zechariah, an elderly priest who was tired of waiting. Zechariah had heard promises of Israel’s rescue from oppression and sin his entire life. That future must have seemed out of reach under Rome’s harsh control. But Zechariah and his wife, Elizabeth, also had an unfulfilled personal longing: “They had no children because Elizabeth was unable to conceive, and they were both very old” ( Luke 1:7, NLT ). One day, as Zechariah performed his duties in the temple, he was chosen to burn incense in the sanctuary — a rare honor with an unexpected result: While Zechariah was in the sanctuary, an angel of the Lord appeared to him, standing to the right of the incense altar. Zechariah was shaken and overwhelmed with fear when he saw him. But the angel said, “Don’t be afraid, Zechariah! God has heard your prayer. Your wife, Elizabeth, will give you a son, and you are to name him John. You will have great joy and gladness, and many will rejoice at his birth, for he will be great in the eyes of the Lord. He must never touch wine or other alcoholic drinks. He will be filled with the Holy Spirit, even before his birth. And he will turn many Israelites to the Lord their God. He will be a man with the spirit and power of Elijah. He will prepare the people for the coming of the Lord. He will turn the hearts of the fathers to their children, and he will cause those who are rebellious to accept the wisdom of the godly” ( Luke 1:11-17, NLT ). Trusting God in the Waiting An angel of the Lord appeared to Zechariah and announced that God had heard his prayer. Elizabeth would have a son named John who would “… prepare the people for the coming of the Lord” ( Luke 1:17b, NLT ). After years of waiting, God answered Zechariah and Elizabeth’s prayer as part of an even bigger story: They would finally have the child they had prayed for, and their son would prepare the way for Jesus. But Zechariah struggled to understand how it could possibly happen: “… ‘How can I be sure this will happen? I’m an old man now, and my wife is also well along in years’” ( Luke 1:18, NLT ). Zechariah could only see what seemed possible based on his circumstances. But God was asking him to trust what He had promised. The angel Gabriel responded by telling Zechariah that he would be unable to speak until the child was born, adding, “For my words will certainly be fulfilled at the proper time” ( Luke 1:20b, NLT ). Maybe you know what it’s like to pray about something for months or even years. It can be hard to keep trusting that God is working when it seems like nothing is changing. Zechariah’s story reminds us that even when we can’t see what God is doing, He is still faithful to His promises. Waiting is woven throughout the Christmas story. Maybe it’s part of your story too. Our free four-week Advent devotional, “Hope in the Waiting,” can help you spend time in Scripture a

title: No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People
source: Wycliffe Bible Translators · 译经故事
summary: See how Bible translation helps communities access more of God’s Word through print, audio and sign language Scripture today.   The post  No Incomplete Stories: God’s Word for All People  appeared first on  Wycliffe .
content: Imagine reading a book, watching a show or listening to a podcast when suddenly the story just stops mid-sentence. Maybe the previous reader has ripped out a page, the series was canceled before the showrunners could wrap up the plotline, or the producer distributed the episode before realizing it was incomplete. How incredibly frustrating to not experience the full story from start to finish! It can leave us emotionally unsettled, frustrated or even distraught, because at our core, we desire completion. We want to know how things start and how they end. We don’t just want a taste, because it feels like a tease. We’re left wanting more . And we’re not alone in that desire! The same is true for communities around the world who are still waiting for the full counsel of God’s Word in a language and format they clearly understand. For some, they’re still waiting for the first verse of Scripture to be translated into their language. Others might have a few verses, chapters or Scripture portions . Still others are blessed with a complete New Testament but are waiting for the Old Testament so they can understand everything from Genesis to Revelation. They get a teaser of God’s great story — perhaps enough to understand who Jesus is and that He died for them — but they don’t have the full context as to why His sacrifice was so significant. The Bible changes everything, and together with our partners, Wycliffe believes that everyone should have access to the whole of Scripture. But don’t just take our word for it! Explore these Bible translation stories from our friends around the world who have personally experienced individual and community transformation as a result of encountering God through His Word. Want a glimpse of what it’s like to only have a portion of God’s Word? This “H ly B bl: Incomplete Scriptures” digital booklet helps you see what it’s like to have gaps in your understanding of the Bible. Explore the booklet → The Full “Outfit” of God’s Word Caroline always had access to a Bible growing up. But watching the Chonyi people of Kenya receive the New Testament in their language refreshed her passion for Bible translation, a mission she’s actively engaged in through SIL Kenya, a partner of Wycliffe. “They took a couple of Bibles, wrapped them up like a child,” she shared. “And there was a woman who was carrying the [Bibles]. And they were swinging and dancing, lifting up the [Bibles] and saying, ‘This is our child.’ Calling people, ‘Come,” in the Chonyi language. ‘Come and celebrate the child that has been born in us.’ “That is how the Chonyi people have taken the Bible — the New Testament — in their own language. That it is their child and they’re taking it seriously, making it bear fruit.” People gathered to hear Scripture read in their language, Bible studies began and the impact spread: 300 adults and 50 children gave their lives to Christ! At the celebration, the local pastors shared that now that the New Testament is complete, it’s like they have a shirt. But a shirt isn’t enough; they want a pair of pants (the Old Testament) to complete the outfit! Now work is underway to translate the Old Testament into Chonyi so that they can have the full “outfit” of God’s Word. Praise God! Watch how the Chonyi community celebrated the dedication of the New Testament in their community! As her neighbors listened alongside her, they became captivated by the story of Jesus. One day, someone from the community called the local translation office with a request. “We have been enjoying this Jesus story from this elderly woman, and now it has broken. title: Lucky Te Koha: The Gang Member Police Officers Prayed For
summary: 🇳🇿Kaikōura· 2017 (gave his life to Christ)
content: A Life in Gangs Lucky Te Koha, a South Islander, was raised by New Zealand's state care system. As a child he was made to stay at Cherry Farm, a state-run mental hospital for adults, a place he remembers plainly: "The abuse in that place was next level." He later found a home in the gang system. Drugs and drink, he says, led to "crime, court cases, police battles, boys' homes, youth prison, prison and rehabs." He moved into an organised crime group, and for 40 years he hated the police. His Third Sunday at Church He began going to Kaikōura New Life Church on New Zealand's South Island. On only his third visit he recognised a police officer who had recently arrested him. During the service Lucky felt intense chest pain. The officer came over and asked if he could pray for him. Four men gathered around him and prayed, and Lucky remembers the chest pain leaving. "I sensed God saying, 'I softened you, giving you a new heart. From here on, you'll feel for others.'" Afterwards he found out that all four men were police officers. His hatred of the police fell away. "I know God delivered me. I sensed that in this house, these were my brothers." Three months from turning 50, he had only ever felt he belonged in gangs, foster homes or prison. "It's a moment only God could've orchestrated." Taking Christ Into Gang Culture Lucky gave his life to Christ in 2017. Under the mentoring of Brian O'Connor, senior pastor of Kaikōura New Life Church, he was ordained in 2019, and in 2021 he founded Kingdom Ministries to take the gospel into gang culture. "Broken people raise broken kids. Hurt people hurt people, but healed people can heal people." God spoke this promise through the prophet Ezekiel: "I will give you a new heart and put a new spirit within you; I will remove your heart of stone and give you a heart of flesh" (Ezekiel 36:26). In a small church in Kaikōura, with four police officers praying around him, Lucky Te Koha heard God say it to him.

title: Juan Alberto: A Security Guard Set Free at His Post
summary: 🇦🇷Buenos Aires· 7 to 8 November 2025 (came to faith); 7 June 2026 (baptised)
content: Twenty-Five Years of Spirit Worship Juan Alberto, 64, lives in Guernica on the outskirts of Buenos Aires, Argentina. For 25 years he practised Quimbanda, an Afro-Brazilian form of spirit worship built around spirit possession and ceremonies that promise success and protection. Tears at the Stadium In November 2025 he was working security at Vélez Sarsfield Stadium for the Esperanza Buenos Aires Festival with Franklin Graham. On the first day, the musicians rehearsing on stage were praising Jesus and singing of His love. Juan Alberto had never heard anything like it. As he listened, the Holy Spirit touched his heart, and he began to weep and could not stop. Soon he felt sick, asked his supervisor if he could go home, and told no one what had happened. The next day his niece Melany, a Christian serving as a prayer volunteer, came to say hello. She told him the Lord had prepared that night for him to feel His love. When Franklin Graham invited people to come forward and receive Jesus, Juan Alberto could not leave his post, so he prayed silently right where he stood. Later that night Melany asked if he had prayed. He said yes, with wet eyes, and told her everything. "He told me he knew and understood that God loved him and forgave him," she said. Idols Burned at His Baptism In the months after the festival he lost his job and his rental home. He kept going to church with Melany at Iglesia Conexión con Dios and joined a small group. On 7 June 2026 he was baptised, and he burned all the idols, garments and spirit-worship objects he had used in Quimbanda. Since then, God has restored his relationships. "I always used to say I was the lost sheep. I never imagined that God would take notice of me," he says. Jesus told of the shepherd who leaves the ninety-nine "and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it" (Luke 15:4). He found Juan Alberto at a security post, in the middle of his shift. "Something extraordinary happened to me. I had an encounter with God, and it was the most beautiful experience of my life."

title: Rakthai Sophia Loibl: Sold as a Child, Brought Back to Life by Jesus
summary: 🇹🇭Bangkok· Over many years before 2025 (published March 2025)
content: A Child Sold in Bangkok Rakthai Sophia Loibl's earliest memory is of crying inside a locked supply room in Thailand. When she was 3, her mother was selling her for a few days at a time as a child labourer. When she was around 4, her mother took her to a home in Bangkok, where a man paid 2,000 baht. Her mother never came back. The man was the imam of the local Muslim community, and Rakthai grew up as his slave labourer. Twice she gave birth to his daughters, and twice the baby was taken from her at once. A Gentle Voice At 25, pregnant for the second time, she began to hear a gentle whisper: It's okay. Just stay alive. "I didn't know who or what this voice was, but it comforted me; it was powerful yet gentle." One night, not long after the second birth, the voice woke her at three in the morning and told her to escape through the window. She did. Later she followed a man to Chicago, where for six and a half years he abused her. She tested positive for HIV and developed tuberculosis. Sent back to Bangkok, she lay in hospital for three months, paralysed, unable to see or to remember her own name. In her heart she cried out to Jesus: If you are with me, come save me. The doctors told her relatives to prepare for a funeral. Afraid she was contagious, they put her in a small house far from their homes in the village to wait for her to die. For six weeks she had only water. Then the voice spoke again: Live. "In that little house, I understood that it had been Jesus' voice all along," she says. "My wounds healed and my spirits lifted." One day she stumbled out of the wooden house, and her family, the villagers and the doctors were shocked. A pastor who had visited her in hospital brought her to a ministry called The Well, and there she gave her life to Jesus. Bread for the Imam God called her back to the community she had escaped, to forgive them and to love them. About eight years later the imam, dying of cancer, phoned and asked to see her. "I sat next to him as he lay bedridden, and he asked me to forgive him." Then he asked for bread and coffee. She remembered Jesus' command to love her enemies, handed him the bread, and felt the chains in her heart break. Before he died, the imam asked if she wanted her daughters back. Both now live with her. Rakthai founded Walk with Love, a Bangkok ministry to people in desperate situations across Thailand. "I am living proof that God is working in the darkness."

title: Maxym Abramov: From Occupied Sloviansk to Army Chaplain
summary: 🇺🇦Sloviansk· 2014 (came to faith); 5 May 2022 (wounded)
content: A City Struck In 2014 Maxym Abramov was a 16-year-old schoolboy in Sloviansk, in eastern Ukraine, getting ready to finish school. On 12 April that year Russia first struck his hometown, and the city was occupied. The occupation shattered the way he saw life. Depression closed in, and it drove him to the edge of suicide. That was when he found Christ. "My material world simply collapsed like a house of cards," he says. Two Metres Away Before he joined the army, Maxym volunteered at a rehabilitation centre for people struggling with addiction. Later he signed a contract with the army. On 5 May 2022, in the third month of the full-scale war, his unit held a stretch of front line under a barrage that lasted more than 12 hours. A fellow soldier sitting two metres behind him was hit in the neck by shrapnel and died instantly. Maxym was wounded in the arm. He was ordered to reach the evacuation point about a kilometre away, and he ran, fell, got up and ran again under fire. At the hospital in Bakhmut the doctors looked at his arm and said things looked grim. "The damage was so severe, I still don't know how God saved it. But He did." A Chaplain Who Listens In December 2024 Maxym became a certified military chaplain. He studies at Kremenchuk Seminary and the Ostroh Academy, and he cares for soldiers, veterans and the families of the fallen, the captured and the missing. "I've earned the right to speak to them about hope," he says. "But more often, my job is simply to listen." God met a teenager at the edge of his life in an occupied city. Eight years later, in a hospital in Bakhmut, He saved the arm the doctors said looked grim. "Even though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil, for You are with me" (Psalm 23:4).

title: Telemachus: The Monk Who Stepped Into the Arena
summary: 🇮🇹Rome· c. AD 404 (traditional date; Theodoret gives none)
content: A Monk From the East Theodoret, a bishop of Cyrrhus in Syria who wrote a history of the Church in the fifth century, recorded this account. A man named Telemachus had "embraced the ascetic life": he was a monk. He left the East and travelled to Rome. Into the Arena In Rome the gladiatorial games still went on. Gladiators fought before crowds for entertainment, and a fight could end in death. From the time of Constantine, imperial laws had put limits on the games, and the fights continued. On a day when the games were on, Telemachus went into the stadium. He stepped down into the arena and tried to stop the men who were fighting each other with their weapons. The crowd was furious. In Theodoret's words, they "stoned the peacemaker to death." What Theodoret Says the Emperor Did When the emperor Honorius heard what had happened, Theodoret writes, he "numbered Telemachus in the array of victorious martyrs, and put an end to that impious spectacle." What Historians Say Theodoret gives no date. Tradition places the event around AD 404, and the Church remembers Telemachus on 1 January. Historians still debate the account. An older list of martyrs records a Roman martyr called Almachius on 1 January, and some scholars think Theodoret's story grew from that record. Others treat the two men as different martyrs. Recent studies also question whether Honorius issued a ban on the games in 404. Remembered Because Someone Wrote It Down Jesus said, "Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called sons of God" (Matthew 5:9). In Theodoret's account, Telemachus has that same name: the peacemaker. Theodoret kept this story, and more than sixteen hundred years after its traditional date, Christians still tell it. It shows what peacemaking can cost: one man saw people kill each other for a crowd's entertainment, and he stepped in to stop it.

title: Arrested at the hospital where he worked, he turned the prison into a pulpit
summary: 🇪🇷Eritrea· 2010s
content: Dr Berhane was a new believer in Jesus, working in a hospital in Eritrea, when the secret police came for him. His crime was his faith. They put him in prison for eleven months, in one of the harshest systems on earth, a place designed to make Christians disappear and go quiet. He did the opposite. "Every day I was clapping my hands," he said, "and prisoners would come forward and I shared the gospel." A man who had only recently met Jesus decided his cell was simply the next place to introduce Him. Three Bibles and a valley of death The authorities took his Bible. He smuggled another in. They took that one too, and he smuggled a third. He leaned hard on the Psalms, and when fellow prisoners were taken out and executed, the old line about walking through the valley of the shadow of death stopped being poetry and became the thing that held him upright. Eleven months of that did not break him. It made him a preacher. The guards meant to silence a new Christian and instead handed him a congregation with nowhere to go. Wherever they put you, Jesus goes with you, and He is not intimidated by the walls. Dr Berhane found that out in an Eritrean prison. You can trust it wherever you are.

title: A construction engineer in Madagascar became convinced the Bible was true
summary: 🇲🇬Madagascar· 2013
content: Melias was building things for a living in Madagascar, a construction engineer with a steady trade and, by his own account, no particular expectation that God would interrupt him. In 2013, at twenty-one, God did. It was not dramatic thunder. It was quieter and harder to argue with. "The Holy Spirit convinced my heart that the Bible is true," Melias said. "I found new joy and excitement learning about Jesus through the Scriptures." The book he might have dismissed became the most alive thing in his life. From building houses to building the church He could have kept his new faith as a private comfort and gone on with engineering. Instead he gave it everything. In 2015 he trained for six months as a missionary, and since then he has planted churches and discipled new believers among the Tanala people in Ikongo and the Sakalava in Nosy Be, some of the least reached corners of the island. Now he is training three more Malagasy missionaries to do the same. Madagascar is not a footnote in what God is doing. He is raising up local people like Melias, engineers and tradesmen and ordinary workers, and sending them to their own unreached neighbours. When the Holy Spirit convinces your heart that this is all true, it does not stay a hobby. It becomes the thing you build your life around. He is ready to convince yours.

title: A New Testament sat in his welding workshop until a teenager finally read it
summary: 🇳🇪Agadez· 2000s
content: Someone left a New Testament in Pierre's welding workshop in Niger, and for a while it just sat there. He was a teenager, and eventually he picked it up. What he read did not match what he had been told about Christians. It was full of tenderness, of nearness to the poorest, exactly the kind of world his young heart had been quietly hoping was real. Years later he moved to Agadez, out toward the desert, and there he found the thing the book had described. A church family drawn from Benin, Togo, Burkina Faso, France, and Niger, living out what he had only read about. No regret, not for a single day Pierre became a lay missionary, and he does not hedge when he talks about it. "I have never regretted converting to the Christian faith," he says, "not even for a single day." That is a bold thing to say in Niger, where jihadist groups make following Jesus dangerous and his own children have stayed Muslim, something he carries with love and without pressure. Still, no regret. Not one day. He read about a God who is tender toward the poor, and he found that God to be exactly as advertised. Whatever you have heard about Jesus secondhand, He holds up when you finally meet Him yourself. Pierre would tell you to open the book and see.

title: He was taught Christians do not pray. Then he watched his uncle pray before a meal
content: Charles Yabaga Diarra grew up in a strict Muslim family in Lere, Mali, where Christians were mocked and misunderstood. His father, a headmaster and politician, ran the house like a school. As a boy, Charles fled about a hundred and fifty miles to stay with an uncle, and there he ran straight into something he had been told did not exist. His uncle, a Christian pastor, bowed his head and prayed before the meal. Charles was stunned. "Because we are Christians, we pray before meals," the uncle explained. Charles had been taught that Christians do not pray at all. That simple prayer, in his own language, lodged in him and would not leave. Just show me the way His father pulled him back and forced him into Quranic school, but the seed was planted. Years later, back with his uncle, tired and searching, Charles finally prayed his own prayer. "Lord, I'm really tired of seeking the truth. Just show me the way." A verse he had heard at a Vacation Bible School came back to him, and in November 1981 he gave his life to Jesus. The cost has been real. Charles is a preacher now, displaced by Mali's conflict and facing daily pressure. But he did not go alone. Of his fourteen siblings, most now follow Jesus, and around a hundred Christians gather at his extended family events. One uncle praying over dinner turned a whole family toward Jesus. Your quiet, ordinary faithfulness may be planting more than you know.

title: A widow heard the good news from a travelling salesman and could not unhear it
summary: Laos· 2022
content: Pei was a fifty-two-year-old widow in Laos, raised the way her whole village was raised, worshipping ancestors and local spirits in a place where the government pushes atheism and neighbours warn that following the God of foreigners will offend the gods of home. Then a salesman came through and, somewhere between selling his goods, told her about Jesus. Salvation as a gift, not a payment. Pei believed it. She let go of the ancestor worship she had carried her whole life and quietly followed Jesus instead. The cost at her own front door She was discipled in secret for four months, growing strong enough to speak. The first people she told were her daughter and her son-in-law, who happens to be a policeman. They did not celebrate. He threatened her, saying that if she did not stop believing in Jesus, they would report her, jail her, or throw her out. In June they made good on it, tossing her clothes into the yard and telling her to go live with the people who gave her this Jesus. She went. She did not go back. A widow with nothing chose Jesus over a roof, because she had found something no one could evict from her heart. Following Jesus is not always safe, but it is always worth it. What Pei found is worth more than what it cost her, and it is offered to you too.

title: After his daughter was killed, he prayed for a Bible no one could take from him
summary: Uzbekistan and Tajikistan· 2020s
content: Rashid Kadirov was a Muslim in Central Asia when the worst thing happened. His six-year-old daughter Azizza was killed by a drunk neighbour driving a tractor. In his grief he went looking for something the ache could rest on, and he went to the Koran. There he read a line, in Surah 5:70, that pointed back to the Gospels as holy scripture. So he prayed a strange, specific prayer. He asked God for an Injil, a New Testament. His friends brought him one. It was a stolen Gideon Bible, taken from a vandalised car. It did not last. When the friends took it back, Rashid prayed again, this time for a Bible no one could take away from him. The book that stayed Then a couple arrived from Tajikistan, sent by a former classmate of his who had himself come to Christ. They carried a Bible and a copy of the JESUS Film. Rashid and his wife Aleka watched it, and as the good news was explained, each of them, without telling the other, quietly prayed to receive Jesus. Aleka barely understood it all. "She had very little understanding of the Gospel," she said later, "and yet peace flooded her heart." They were baptised in Tajikistan, and Rashid started telling others what he had found. A grieving father asked for a book, and God gave him a Person. The peace Rashid could not manufacture arrived the moment Jesus did. He is close to the brokenhearted, and He is near to you.

title: 35 priests could not help her. In a church she saw Jesus crush what was choking her
summary: 🇱🇰North Central Province· 2021
content: Chandra lived in a rural village in Sri Lanka's North Central Province, and she was slowly falling apart. Pain, weakness, a heart that raced for no reason doctors could name. She and her family were Hindu, so they did what they knew to do. They went to priest after priest. Thirty-five of them. Nothing changed. In July 2021 they walked into a church instead. As people prayed for her, Chandra saw something. Demons were trying to strangle her, and then Jesus Christ stepped in and stamped on them. She felt the pain and the sickness drain out of her body as they were defeated. In the vision Jesus spoke Scripture over her, from Psalm 34. "They looked to Him and were radiant," He said, and told her she would be radiant too if she trusted Him. The prayer a father prayed Her husband Dinesh, a day labourer, watched his wife come back to life and made God a promise. "God, if you will heal my wife, I will dedicate my daughter for your service." The whole family, who had barely heard the name of Jesus, gave their lives to Him. Their daughter Tenusha told her class what had happened, that her mother was free and that Jesus forgives sinners and makes them new. They did not keep it to themselves. A house church started in their home with four people. By now it is forty-six. Jesus is still stronger than whatever is choking the life out of you. He steps in, He stamps it down, and He calls you radiant.

title: He prayed for his mother's infected leg. Then his Muslim neighbours started coming
summary: 🇸🇩El Hasahisa· 2022
content: Pastor Abdalla Haron Sulieman gathered his small church in El Hasahisa, Sudan, to pray for his mother. Aisha Adam was sixty, and a leg infection had worn her down. They prayed, and she recovered. What looked like a private family mercy did not stay private for long. Word of the healing moved through the town, which is mostly Muslim. And people started showing up at the church. Not to argue. To ask if the God who healed Aisha might heal them too. When a healing becomes a door That is exactly the kind of thing that makes some people afraid. Local extremists pressed the police to arrest Sulieman, and they did, charging him under an old law with claiming to be a witch doctor, as if the love of Jesus were a kind of sorcery. Believers across Sudan shared his name and called for his release. "This is a serious violation against Christians in Sudan," said one, an evangelist named Francis Ismail. But notice what the fear could not undo. A mother was well. A Muslim town had seen the name of Jesus do something real, and neighbours who had never entered a church walked in looking for Him. God still heals, and He still uses one ordinary answered prayer to open a door no one can shut. He can open one where you are too.

title: Karma said he had to earn heaven. At 17 he heard he could be forgiven
summary: Rakiraki· 1990s
content: Simon Gounder was born into a strict Hindu family in Fiji. His great-grandfather had been shipped from India as a contract labourer after the British took the islands in 1874, and the family settled in a small village in the north of Viti Levu. Simon grew up inside a system with clear rules. "As a Hindu, we believed in karma," he said. "If you do good karma, you get to heaven. If you do bad karma, you will be punished." It was a ledger he could never quite balance. He knew his own wrongs too well. The night the ledger closed At seventeen, a friend invited him to a Christian youth meeting in another town. There he heard something that did not fit anything he had been taught. That Jesus Christ could simply forgive sins. Not offset them, not average them out over lifetimes. Forgive them. Simon felt the weight of his own failures and, for the first time, an offer to be free of them. "I gave my life to Jesus that night," he said. He hid it from his parents at first. When they found out, they were not happy. But the son who came home changed did not stop there. In time he led his whole family to Christ, and he went on to plant a ministry that carries the same forgiveness to others. Karma keeps a running tab you can never clear. Jesus tears the tab up. Whatever you are carrying tonight, He is still in the business of forgiving it all at once.

title: A soldier who should have died in battle walked into a demon's shrine
summary: 🇲🇲Myanmar· 2010s
content: Pastor Dano was a soldier before he was a pastor. He came out of the battlefield alive when he had no reason to, and he never shook the sense of why. "I believe God preserved my life from death on the battlefield for a purpose," he said. The purpose showed up in a Buddhist village that wanted nothing to do with him. The vice chief's son was tormented, demon-possessed, and no one could help. Dano fasted and prayed for three days. Then, near midnight, he went to the shrine where the boy was and did the only thing he knew to do. "I called upon the name of the Lord," he said, "and the demon left the young man." The night the shrines fell silent Villagers said every evil spirit left the village at once. Dano went from shrine to shrine, praying against the darkness that had ruled the place for generations. The vice chief's family, who had braced for his anger, found grace instead. They gave their lives to Jesus, and four more families followed. The people who once opposed him now follow his lead. There is a church in that village today where there used to be shrines. The name of Jesus is still stronger than every dark thing that has ever frightened you. One believer, praying at midnight, was enough to set a whole village free.

title: En 2023 , Francisco organizó su sucesión : Puso a Prevost en el lugar idóneo por si soplaba el Espíritu Santo en esa dirección …
summary: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que termi
content: Antes de escribir la biografía de Jorge Bergoglio, que llamó El gran Reformador, Austen Ivereigh ya era un experto en la historia de la Iglesia argentina. “Mi tesis de doctorado [en Oxford], que terminé en el 92, fue sobre catolicismo y política en la Argentina”. Y hay más: “Debo mi fe a la Iglesia Argentina, leyendo artículos de monseñor (Gustavo) Franceschi, volví a la fe”, dice. Ese conocimiento de nuestro país y de su fe mayoritaria representó una ventaja a la hora de escribir sobre Bergoglio, ya que cada etapa de la trayectoria del futuro Papa está debidamente contextualizada en la época que atravesaba el país. Desde aquel marzo de 2013, cuando la novedad de un pontífice argentino y jesuita impactó al mundo entero, Ivereihg siempre pensó que vendría cuando Francisco visitara la Argentina, viaje que finalmente no se concretó. “Ahora vengo con León”, comenta. En efecto, este escritor, historiador, periodista y analista de asuntos religiosos y políticos estará en nuestro país contemporáneamente con la visita del papa León XIV, invitado por la Universidad del Salvador (USAL), donde dictó, el pasado viernes 6, una clase magistral sobre “El giro latinoamericano Francisco-León: la Iglesia misionera sinodal y el cambio de época”. Ivereigh también es co-autor de Let Us Dream (Soñemos Juntos, 2020), un libro escrito en colaboración con Francisco. Su trabajo más reciente es First Belong to God: On Retreat with Pope Francis (Lo primero es pertenecer a Dios: Un retiro con el Papa Francisco, 2024), basado en los escritos y charlas de Bergoglio como director espiritual de un retiro ignaciano de 8 días. De 2004 a 2006, Ivereigh fue colaborador del entonces arzobispo de Westminster, cardenal Cormac Murphy-O’Connor, uno de los más activos promotores de la candidatura de Jorge Mario Bergoglio al papado. Ivereigh considera que el papado de Francisco inició un giro latinoamericano hacia una iglesia misionera y sinodal, cuyo primer paso fue la exhortación apostólica Evangelii Gaudium (noviembre de 2013), sobre “el anuncio del Evangelio en el mundo actual”, con la cual, dice, “Francisco inaugura una hoja de ruta de su Papado que también es la del pontificado de León”. Pero esa hoja de ruta tenía una génesis anterior: el ya famoso documento de Aparecida, la V Conferencia General del Episcopado Latinoamericano y del Caribe (Celam), redactado por Bergoglio. De esta manera, “América Latina pasó a ser la iglesia fuente”, señala, porque “siempre hay una parte de la Iglesia de la cual brota un dinamismo teológico”. Antes, ese rol lo cumplía Europa, pero a partir del Concilio Vaticano II eso cambia porque es en América Latina donde mejor se lo pone en práctica. Aclara que “fuente” no quiere decir centro; de hecho, “Francisco quería una Iglesia multipolar”. — ¿Hasta qué punto Aparecida refleja a Bergoglio como individualidad y hasta dónde es la Iglesia latinoamericana, que usted define como “fuente”? — El proceso de preparación de esa conferencia general, fue muy sinodal, de mucha consulta, y el papel de Bergoglio en esa conferencia general es muy conocido. Creo que influyó la recepción del Concilio Vaticano II en el Río de La Plata, que tuvo un matiz distinto al resto de América Latina. Tal vez, cuando llegó a Aparecida esa visión sobre la religiosidad popular estaba ya madura. Es decir, una teología de espiritualidad latinoamericana, distinta a anteriores teologías latinoamericanas. Bergoglio tenía muchas cosas que eran de él. Pero también llevaba en su forma de ser y de pensar muchos aportes de la iglesia argentina, la influencia de Lucio Gera y de Rafael Tello y toda esa tradición. — ¿Cómo vio el impacto de su papado en la Argentina? — Creo que una de las razones por las que no vino, sobre todo al principio, fue que tenía horror del triunfalismo. Y sabía que tal vez los argentinos tenían —todos los países lo tienen— una cierta tentación de decir: “El Papa es argentino”. Y si le tenía tanto rechazo al triunfalismo, era porque éste pone a uno en el ce

title: Il Mimmo Beneventano a padre Zanotelli , Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista - Notizie
summary: Saranno assegnati a padre Alex Zanotelli, al giornalista Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista (consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista) i riconoscimenti dell'edizione
content: Saranno assegnati a padre Alex Zanotelli, al giornalista Leo Amato e alla memoria di Massimo Battista (consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista) i riconoscimenti dell'edizione 2026 del 'Riconoscimento Nazionale Mimmo Beneventano', la cui cerimonia di premiazione è in programma sabato prossimo, 14 novembre, a Sasso di Castalda (Potenza). Ne ha dato notizia Libera Basilicata, ricordando che "il 7 novembre è una data che porta con sé una ferita ancora aperta, ma anche una testimonianza che il tempo non ha cancellato. In questo giorno del 1980, a Ottaviano, veniva assassinato dalla camorra Mimmo Beneventano, giovane medico, consigliere comunale e uomo impegnato nella difesa della propria comunità dalle infiltrazioni e dalle speculazioni della criminalità organizzata. Beneventano - è ricordato nel comunicato - aveva scelto di non voltarsi dall'altra parte, opponendosi apertamente agli interessi della Nuova Camorra Organizzata e pagando con la vita il proprio impegno. A distanza di 46 anni, il suo esempio continua a rappresentare un riferimento per quanti credono nella democrazia, nella libertà, nella giustizia sociale e nella necessità di contrastare ogni forma di sopraffazione mafiosa. È proprio nel segno di questa eredità civile e morale che sabato 14 novembre, a Sasso di Castalda, paese caro a Mimmo per le origini familiari e nel cui cimitero riposa, si terrà il XVIII Riconoscimento Nazionale Mimmo Beneventano, appuntamento annuale dedicato a valorizzare l'impegno di donne e uomini che, attraverso il proprio lavoro e le proprie scelte, contribuiscono ad affermare i valori della democrazia e della legalità contro le mafie e la corruzione". Per l'edizione 2026 "i riconoscimenti saranno assegnati a tre personalità provenienti da ambiti diversi, ma accomunate da percorsi di impegno civile e professionale. Padre Alex Zanotelli, missionario comboniano e giornalista, è una figura di riferimento nel panorama dell'impegno sociale e della cooperazione internazionale. Per anni ha vissuto a Korogocho, una delle baraccopoli di Nairobi, condividendo la quotidianità delle comunità più povere. È stato direttore della rivista Nigrizia e successivamente di Mosaico di pace, distinguendosi per la sua attività di denuncia e per le battaglie sui temi della pace, del disarmo, della giustizia sociale e dell'acqua come bene comune. Massimo Battista, al quale il riconoscimento sarà conferito alla memoria, è stato consigliere comunale di Taranto, operaio dell'ex Ilva e attivista. Ha legato il proprio percorso personale e pubblico alle vicende della città di Taranto, impegnandosi nelle questioni riguardanti il mondo del lavoro, la salute dei cittadini e la tutela ambientale. La sua figura resta legata alle battaglie civili e sociali del territorio tarantino. Leo Amato, giornalista, ha svolto una parte significativa della propria attività professionale in Basilicata, collaborando con Il Quotidiano del Sud, per poi proseguire il suo percorso anche a livello nazionale nella redazione de Il Fatto Quotidiano. Nel corso della sua carriera si è occupato di cronaca, politica e inchieste, seguendo da vicino vicende e questioni di interesse pubblico legate ai territori. Tre storie e tre percorsi che saranno al centro della cerimonia di quest'anno, nel solco dei valori che hanno contraddistinto la vita di Mimmo Beneventano". Riproduzione riservata © Copyright ANSA

title: A La Carte (November 27)
summary: Is it ever right to pay a bribe? / The problem of the person who shouts loudest / Six reasons Christians can give thanks in every circumstance / What John Piper gets wrong about scrupulosity / Thankful for evangelical publishing / Christmas is not in the Bible / Black Friday deals / The funnies See Also Black Friday & Cyber Monday 2013 Deals for Christians A La Carte (November 29) Black Friday Kindle Deals for the Christian Reader
content: It’s Black Friday today, so I spent a long time yesterday working my way through the various deals that come with it. You can find them in a few different places: Black Friday 2026 Deals for Christians is the general list, Black Friday Book Deals for Christians lists printed books, and Black Friday Kindle Deals for Christians lists Kindle deals. I hope you’ll find something that catches your eye. Also, if you missed it earlier this week, I created A Gift Guide for the Christian Reader on Your List . Sales & Deals It’s a massive day for Kindle deals , and among them you’ll find Essentials of Reformed Systematic Theology by Beeke & Smalley, Tim Keller on the Christian Life by Smethurst, Grasping God’s Word by Duvall & Hays, Biblical Critical Theory by Watkin, and much more. You can check the normal deals page, but should also check in with this one: Black Friday Kindle Deals for Christians . Recommended Reading Is It Ever Right to Pay a Bribe? Paul Schlehlein explains the difference between extortion and bribery. He believes Christians must never extort or bribe anyone, but that paying up when you are the one being extorted is not a sin. “The topic of ethics answers the question: which activities are right or wrong? More specifically, Christian ethics answers the question: which actions does the Bible say please God? May the State execute murderers by lethal injection? Should marijuana be outlawed? May a woman fill her lips with Botox? Is birth control valid? What about tattoos, vaccines, assisted suicide, and AR-15s? All of these are ethical questions.” Pastoral Care: The Problem of the Person Who Shouts Loudest. Al Gooderham: “I used to be a teacher and as every teacher will be aware you often miss the quiet kids in the middle. There’s the high flyers, the kids who need extension work and developing in terms of holistic thinking about what you’re teaching. Then there’s the kids you have to watch like a hawk, because they could derail the whole lesson, they occupy a disproportionate amount of your time because in part they often shout loudest. They’re the ones with their hand up, with the silly question, with another thing that means they need to monopolise your time. The same can be true in our pastoral care as churches.” Six Reasons Christians Can Give Thanks in Every Circumstance. It may be the day after Thanksgiving, but it’s still a good day to give thanks. To that end, Robb Brunansky provides six reasons Christians can give thanks to God no matter their circumstances. What John Piper Gets Wrong About Scrupulosity. John Piper recently addressed scrupulosity in an episode of Ask Pastor John. I find Alan Noble’s response helpful in understanding the plight of someone who suffers with it. Though he affirms much of what Piper says, he writes that “Piper fundamentally misunderstands the nature of OCD thoughts, categorizing them as temptations rather than ego-dystonic intrusions. From this error flows misguided advice about ‘avoiding triggers’ and directing your thoughts through will power. My fear is that this article, while well intentioned, will cause harm to those who are suffering.” Why I’m Thankful for Evangelical Publishing. As one who is very thankful for Evangelical publishing, I appreciate Andrew Spencer’s celebration of the publishers that serve us so well. “English-speaking Christians need to work to preserve the publishers that serve us well. Even confessional and mission-driven publishers have to respond to market signals. If evangelical Christians don’t buy and read the good books being published, the list of future titles will shrink. If we don’t recommend the books we love and critique the ones we don’t, they’ll publish whatever they like or whatever sells. It usually takes much longer to build an institution than to lose one.” Christmas Is Not in the Bible So Your Celebration Doesn’t Measure Your Spirituality. Every year, Stephen Kneale makes sure to remind us that Christmas isn’t in the Bible, so the way you c

title: A La Carte (November 26)
summary: Evangelicalism and ‘high’ culture / Reflection on a public memorial service / The Pilgrims did not invent Thanksgiving / Finding contentment / Are we asking too much of our kids? / Do we have a spirit of entitlement or a spirit of gratitude? / Kindle deals and more See Also A La Carte (November 27) A La Carte (November 20) A La Carte (November 29)
content: Happy Thanksgiving to my American friends and family. I pray you have a restful and thankful day. As you feast, I’ll be prepping a roundup of Black Friday deals that are of interest to Christians, so be sure to check in tomorrow for that. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include the repackaged edition of J.I. Packer’s classic A Quest for Godliness , Tim Chester’s Isaiah for You , Brant Hansen’s Blessed Are the Misfits , and more. Recommended Reading Evangelicalism and ‘High’ Culture. Michael Jensen writes about the lack of Evangelical influence in high culture. “There’s good reasons for this absence. The instinct of true Christianity is thoroughly egalitarian, in recognition of the significance of every human individual and the universal appeal of the gospel. Elitism is abhorrent to true Christianity and especially to missionary Christianity. As Davison Hunter says, ‘elitism for believers is despicable and utterly anathema to the gospel they cherish’.” Reflection on a Public Memorial Service. Kraig Keck tells movingly about his experience at a public memorial service for two police officers who were killed in the line of duty. “Each element of the memorial service evoked powerful emotions in me. As I sat there I was struck by the dignity and honor of it all, and I wondered how a committed atheist evolutionist would understand this. I’m sure he would try to find some evolutionary purpose for it all, but it seemed to me that it would be ultimately unexplainable by his worldview. Why the ceremony, the quiet, the traditions, the dignity, and the honor of it all?” The Pilgrims Did Not Invent Thanksgiving. Allen C. Guelzo reminds American readers that the Pilgrims were not the ones who invented Thanksgiving. “To be sure, the Massachusetts Pilgrims probably did host a harvest dinner in 1621 to mark their survival through their first year in America. But the Thanksgiving we celebrate annually in November had its real origins much closer to the present, and its real designer not in William Bradford or William Brewster, but in the sixteenth president of the United States, Abraham Lincoln.” Quarters and Contentment. Marie Garreau explains how she has sometimes found it easier to be content during times of extreme distress than during “normal” difficulties. “The Lord gave me contentment in that season of extreme need, while in times of lesser need I have found it easier to slip from the confidence of his provision. Perhaps I lose sight of the fact that it is not just in extreme times of need that the circumstances of our lives are completely out of our own hands.” Are We Asking Too Much of Our Kids? Beth Barthelemy asks a question a lot of Christian parents wonder about, and perhaps especially those in missions or other forms of ministry: Are we asking too much of our kids? “As full-time ministry workers, my husband and I have anticipated and accepted all kinds of sacrifices on behalf of working for the kingdom. For our years overseas, those sacrifices looked like family, a sense of security, and cultural familiarity, among others. In pastoral ministry now, these sacrifices are financial, relational, and of our time. We are still discovering others.” Do We Have a Spirit of Entitlement or a Spirit of Gratitude? Randy Alcorn: “Ingratitude is not just wrong thinking—it’s the source of endless wrong thinking. An ungrateful person not only offends God, but is also the source of his own misery, and a cancer to others, spreading his misery. Ungrateful people are not only ungrateful to God but to their families and friends and co-workers and neighbors. They’re ungrateful to their church leaders, and quick to judge and condemn everyone for falling short of their standards.” Flashback Proven Faith Is More Precious than Gold. It can be difficult to make sense of our trials as we endure them. But the Bible always assures us that our difficulties are never purposeless but always in some way purposeful.
