summary: Cultivating thankfulness in a difficult season / The “silent death act” / How to spot a false teacher / American culture and hostility to Christ / Pain reminds us / How to listen to a sermon / Kindle deals and more. See Also A La Carte (April 24) A La Carte (August 29) Kindle Deals for Christian Readers
content: Good morning, my friends. May the Lord be with you and bless you today. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include books for parents and others who care for children, along with a few other titles that may be of interest. Remember that there’s a large Kindle sale until Black Friday that I’ve linked to separately . Over at Westminster Books, you can find a Black Friday Commentary Set Sale . Recommended Reading Cultivating Thankfulness in a Difficult Season. Here is counsel on being thankful even in a difficult season (from a writer who is in one himself). “Even as dedicated Christians, we can be subtly tempted to think like pagans. If I go to church every week, then God will bless me. If I read my Bible and pray every day, God will bless me. If I tithe to my church, or give generously to the Salvation Army, or pack a shoebox for a child overseas, God will bless me. If I go on a short-term mission trip, God will bless me. If I volunteer in the children’s ministry, God will bless me. If I lead a small group, God will bless me.” The “Silent Death Act” in Canada. Barton J. Gingerich describes some of what’s happening in Canada now as the government pushes hard to permit advance directives for euthanasia. “Canada keeps trying to win the dubious honor of the Medical Assistance in Dying (MAID) capital of the world. The Great White North’s plunge into medically assisted suicide continues onto a new frontier. The Canadian government introduced a bill that allows people to request euthanasia at a later date when they have lost the capacity to make that decision, such as in the case of dementia or Alzheimer’s disease. The bill allows patients to be killed even if they appear distressed, are unable to communicate, or have changed their behavior in ways that might suggest a change of mind.” How to Spot a False Teacher. Spotting a false teacher is a crucial skill for a Christian to develop. “What makes this challenging is that while some false teachers and false teaching is obvious, oftentimes it is not. It takes true spiritual discernment to identify true from false teachers/teaching. While there is no magic formula, I would say there are at least 6 indicators to look for and be mindful of as you seek to discern what is true from what is false:” American Culture and Hostility to Christ. Casey McCall: “In America, it’s customary to follow prayers for the persecuted church around the world with prayers of thanksgiving to God that we don’t have to face such harsh resistance here. We rightly thank God for religious liberty and remember those who suffered in past ages to guarantee the freedoms we so enjoy. We praise God that when we gather to worship Jesus on Sundays, we do so without having to worry about violence or arrest. Our experience of security and safety has not always been the experience of Christians in history, and it is not the experience of many today. We ought to be grateful for that.” But maybe there are other forms of danger to be aware of. Pain Reminds Us We Have a Foot in Two Worlds. “Perhaps the best place on earth to see the commonality of humankind in their pain is the emergency room. Walk in there, and it suddenly ceases to matter if you’re rich or poor, black or white, clean or dirty. The ER is one of those places where the stark but often unspoken reality of the desperateness of our situation comes to the surface. And there’s nothing like desperation to focus your prayers.” Michael Kelley offers his thoughts on pain and the way it reminds us that we have a foot in two worlds. How to Listen to a Sermon. I suppose we could all use reminders from time to time on how to listen to sermons well. That’s the purpose of this article from Jacques Nel. “When we evaluate various churches, including our own, perhaps we consider as of first importance the quality of the sermons that are preached. However, good preaching is not the only important thing. It is just as important for us all, the members of the congregation, to listen well

content: Tuesday is the day most publishers release their new books, so each week I let you know what has just come our way from the publishers I follow most closely. It is a quiet week because of Thanksgiving, but there are still a few noteworthy books. Paul David Tripp’s Do You Believe? returns in a new edition with study questions, and Reformation Heritage Books has drawn a year of morning and evening readings from Wilhelmus à Brakel’s The Christian’s Reasonable Service . You’ll find more besides these. For each of them, I’ve included the publisher’s description and a list of the book’s endorsers. (Reminder: Last week was a huge week for new releases, so be sure to check it out if you missed it.) Books for Everyone Crossway Do You Believe? 12 Historic Doctrines to Change Your Everyday Life (with Study Questions) Paul David Tripp Publisher’s description Doctrine—what Christians believe—directly influences how they live. The biblical truths about God, humanity, and the world are not merely about knowing more—they are also about loving God and making sense of this life and the life to come. But what happens when there is disparity between what believers confess and how they live? In the bestselling book Do You Believe? pastor and author Paul David Tripp takes a close look at 12 core doctrines and how they engage and transform the human heart and mind. According to Tripp, “true belief is always lived.” To demonstrate, he unpacks each doctrine and presents its relevance for the Christian life. As readers explore topics such as the doctrine of God, the holiness of God, and the doctrine of Scripture, they will be fueled to fall deeper in love with and stand in awe of their Creator and Father—putting the truths of God’s word on display for all the world to see. This edition includes a section of engaging study questions to guide individuals and groups into deeper reflection. Buy it at Amazon or Westminster Books . Grace Publications Thinking Pastorally A Ministry Miscellany Andrew Roycroft Publisher’s description In the busyness of pastoral ministry, it can be a relief to have a resource which provides short-form encouragement and stimulation, a volume that meets us at the beginning or the close of our days and speaks to us about the challenges and blessings of the work in which we are engaged. Thinking Pastorally is designed to meet this need. Taking the form of a miscellany, it ranges across many of the personal and public issues that attend serving the Lord Jesus Christ. This is a medicine cabinet for ministers whose souls are spiritually weary, a place of respite for battle-worn soldiers persevering in the fight of faith, and a clarion call to pursue and serve Jesus more fully through every season until he returns. Buy it at Amazon . Baker Books Hidden in Jesus Prayers from the Persecuted Church in China Edited by Hannah Nation and Yang Guo, translated by Alicia Akins Publisher’s description The prayers of the Chinese house churches have been shaped by suffering, marginalization, and persecution. They have an urgency that invites us all to understand that the power of prayer goes beyond what we imagine. This collection of prayers, translated into English for the first time, offers a window into the Chinese house church experience. These prayers will teach you how to pray with faith and fervor. They will remind you of your unbreakable union with the triumphant Christ, even in the thickest darkness. title: A La Carte (November 24)
summary: Sisters, aging is not our enemy / With Christ in the singularity / The future of complementarianism / What happened at the Evangelical Theological Society? / Can we have assurance of salvation today? / The surprises that await in heaven / Kindle deals, new books, and more See Also A La Carte (November 27) A La Carte (November 29) A La Carte (November 27)
content: Good morning, and thanks for reading A La Carte. I know many Americans will be tuning out of the internet over the next couple of days as they celebrate Thanksgiving. Just know I will be monitoring Black Friday sales that may be of interest to you, so be sure to check in on Friday to see what I’ve come up with. Sales & Deals Today’s Kindle deals include a couple of very new books, both of which I recommend: Young Womanhood by Amy DiMarcangelo and Talk About What Matters Most by Alasdair Groves. Recommended Reading Sisters, Aging Is Not Our Enemy. Kathryn Butler writes for middle-aged women who are being pummeled with the same messaging she is. “As we age, how do we calibrate our vision to God’s? How do we look into the mirror, perceive every crevice, laugh-line, and blotch, and then respond with deeper joy in the one whose mercy has granted us every year and silvery strand? Sisters, here are four ways to view our changing appearance through the lens of heaven.” With Christ in the Singularity. “Singularity. If you haven’t heard the term, it’s the idea that technology (especially AI) will get so smart and improve itself so fast that the world changes in ways we can’t really imagine or keep up with. If you picture a free-fall picking up speed toward an unknown destination, you’re not far off. Why do I care? And why should you? Good questions.” Kara Dedert takes them on. Four Voices on the Future of Complementarianism. I was interested to read these four different voices each providing their take on the future of complementarianism. “Once a clear biblical response to evangelical feminism, the label of complementarianism is now often used to cover an increasingly wide spectrum. Some narrow versions confine male-female distinction to a handful of biblical texts regarding the church and home. The spectrum of more broad accounts root such differences as a feature of creation order, in nature itself, expect to see application of these differences across the social realm, and, in some cases, give outright calls for a biblical patriarchy where men rule in the home, church, and society. In this set of essays, four men wrestle with the same question from different instincts and positions: Where should complementarianism go from here? “ What Happened at the Evangelical Theological Society? Speaking of complementarianism, it appears to have been one of the themes of last week’s ETS. I always enjoy reading Denny Burk’s post-ETS thoughts, and this year’s installment was no exception. Can We Have Assurance of Salvation Today? I know so many Christians who struggle with assurance of salvation. Perhaps some of them can find comfort in this article by Cornelis Venema. The Surprises That Await in Heaven. Melissa considers and anticipates what may be some of the surprises that await us in heaven. “When we get to Heaven after years of struggle, after levels of exhaustion that we weren’t sure we would survive, when the battle is finally over and we enter into His rest, I believe we’ll be surprised to learn how gloriously God changed the hearts of people through our difficulties. He is working, even now, in the hardest times, in the longest wars, in the greatest failures and in the deepest longings of broken hearts. Nothing is wasted, and one day we’ll see how all of the struggles fit into the plans He made before time ever began.” New Books New Christian books tend to release on Tuesdays. Here are just a few of the books that have become available today. For a more thorough list visit This Week in Christian Books . Do You Believe?: 12 Historic Doctrines to Change Your Everyday Life (with Study Questions) by Paul David Tripp. This is a new edition of Paul Tripp’s look at 12 core Christian doctrines. Thinking Pastorally by Andrew Roycroft. I was pleased to be able to provide a foreword to Andrew Roycroft’s “Ministry Miscellany”—a book pastors will enjoy and value. content: This week, the blog is sponsored by Doxa Games . This post is written by Marco Bartholomae, founder of Doxa Games and creator of the Bible-based board and card games Trials & Triumphs , Bible Clash , and Hurry! Fleeing Disciples . A couple of years ago, I was playing cards with my kids when a question hit me. What would it take to make a Bible game they’d ask to play again? I grew up in Germany with four brothers. We played cards on long car rides and spent hours on our bedroom floor with a board game spread out between us. I still remember how easy it was to lose track of time when we played together. Now I live in California with my wife and our four children, and we still love a good game night. The screens go away, somebody wants a rematch, and we get to enjoy being together. That question from the card table stayed with me. I started imagining games that could give other families that same experience and get them talking about Scripture along the way, games a child could sit down to, learn the rules, and enjoy right away, even if they were new to the Bible. Then maybe a name on a card or something that happened on the board would make them curious enough to ask a question. That’s how Doxa Games started. The Conversations That Start Around the Table In Deuteronomy 6, God tells his people to speak about his commandments with their children as they go about ordinary life, including when they sit at home. A game night gives us another chance to do that. Our games don’t replace family devotions, but they do open conversations about God’s Word. Your child might pick up a card and ask who Thaddaeus was. A race to a house church might get them wondering why the early Christians gathered in homes. Those are questions you can follow right back to Scripture. That’s also why I chose the name Doxa . It’s the Greek word for glory . In 1 Corinthians 10:31, Paul reminds us to do everything to the glory of God, even in ordinary things like eating and drinking. That conviction shapes what we make and how we think about time around the table. Three Games to Play With Your Family Bible Clash: Gospels (ages 8+) is a fast-paced, head-to-head card game. Play characters from the four Gospels and try to outscore your opponent. Trials & Triumphs (ages 5+) sends players down a winding path where one turn can move you forward, and the next can set you back. It gives younger kids a way to talk about trusting Christ through trials. Hurry! Fleeing Disciples (ages 8+) takes you into the world of Acts. Choose your route, evade Roman guards, and race to reach a house church. From Our Family Table to the Mission Field As Doxa grows, we hope to translate these games and put them in the hands of missionaries, church planters, and ministry training centers in places like Colombia, the Philippines, and East Africa. I’d love for a family in Malawi to pull out one of these games, play it in their own language, and have the same kinds of conversations we have around our table. If your family is getting together this Christmas, pick a game, clear a spot at the table, and let the kids make the first move. See all three games at DoxaGames.com . title: The Empty Chair, the Ache, the Tear
summary: Six years after Nick died, his possessions still fill three bins in our basement. Twice a year I see them and am thankful for what they represent and what they make me long for. See Also A Slave to Sin A La Carte (5/8) Captivity
content: Those who live in a cold-weather climate will be familiar with the twice-yearly ritual of swapping summer clothes for winter and winter clothes for summer. Sometime around November, we pull the clear Rubbermaid bins from their shelves in the basement, then unpack the toques, 1 gloves, fleece-lined boots, and heavy coats before repacking them with the out-of-season raincoats, baseball caps, running shoes, and sandals. We reverse the ritual in April or May—whenever we have finally enjoyed the kind of consistent warmth that heralds the arrival of spring and the coming of summer. It took some time after our son Nick’s death before we could clean out his room and begin to either dispose of his possessions or give them away. There were many we could not bring ourselves to purge, so we packed them into that same style of bin and stacked them on those same shelves. Now, twice a year I find myself catching glimpses of the bits and pieces of his life. To anyone else, these bins might seem to contain a random collection of clothes, gadgets, and paraphernalia, yet we associate every one of them with him. There’s a piggy bank shaped like a safe whose bell would ring whenever the girls playfully attempted to pillage it. There’s a selection of books that he read and reread: Tintin , Calvin & Hobbes , and a few volumes considerably more serious. There’s a sweater that looked especially handsome on him and, of course, his ever-present Blue Jays hat . There’s nothing of any real value, yet it’s invaluable to us. It’s a life reduced to three 14-gallon bins. I expect those bins will still be stacked on the shelves when Aileen and I die or need to move out of our home. I expect they will have all the same objects in them. We have learned that what is not purged immediately is likely to be kept indefinitely, for our attachment has only grown through the years. To throw them out or to give them away seems more disloyal today than it would have been six years ago . In fact, we can barely even allow ourselves to open those bins or to touch their contents. It’s just too painful to come into contact with all these things that remind us of a person who was once so much a part of our lives. Nick still is a part of our lives, I suppose, but in a different way. He’s no longer the son who delights us with his wit and impresses us with his brilliance. He’s no longer the son who checks in with Aileen when I’m traveling far from home or who is on call when I have questions about Greek or Hebrew. He’s the empty chair during the holidays, the ache when I think of happier times, the tear that springs to my eyes when we stand in church to sing of the future . He’s the lump in my throat when I consider Christ’s return and the joy that thrills my heart when I ponder heaven. He’s present still, but in a way that is as different as day is from night and pleasure is from pain. I’m thankful that we kept these items, these traces of his existence and reminders of what he used, wore, and enjoyed. I’m thankful that in their own way they remind me of him and all the joy he brought to our lives. I’m grateful that they cause me to long for the day when we leave them all behind, probably still in those Rubbermaid bins, and depart this world as Nick did—with nothing but the faith God has given us and the assurance that he will receive us. In that way, these valueless objects are immeasurably precious. Pronounced tewk (rhymes with duke ), this is a uniquely Canadian word for a winter hat (or what some refer to as a beanie). ↩︎ See Also A Slave to Sin A La Carte (5/8) Captivity

content:
한국교회언론회(대표 심하보 목사)에서 2025년 인구주택총조사 발표에 대한 논평을 11월 27일 발표했다.

교회언론회는 “문제는 다음 세대이다. 각 종교별 1-39세 종교인구는 기독교 289만 2,400명이고, 천주교가 91만 3,819명이며, 불교는 85만 1,349명이다. 그런데 기독교의 경우 10년 전보다 10-18% 이상 젊은 세대에서 빠져나갔다”며 “이제 다음 세대를 위해 한국교회가 ‘올인’할 때가 됐다”고 전했다.

이들은 “이것은 한 교회나 교단만의 문제가 아니라, 한국교회 전체가 참여하고 협력해 청년 세대의 고민과 갈등, 그들의 내면을 치유하고 삶의 의미에 답을 줄 수 있는 체계를 만들어 가야 한다”며 “앞으로 사회학, 인구통계학, 기술 발전 관점에서 탈종교화는 여전히 가속될 것이다. 그러나 영적 존재나 초월적 존재를 믿는 현상(Spirituality)에 대한 요구는 더해질 것”이라고 전망했다.

또 “미래 세대는 아무리 과학과 기술과 복지 제도가 발전한다 해도, 인간의 근본적이고 종교적 질문인 ‘Why(왜)’에 대한 영역은 오히려 또렷해질 것”이라며 “우리 기독교는 여기에 해답을 제시할 수 있어야 하고, 이를 철저하게 준비해야 한다”고 제언했다. 다음은 논평 전문.

2025년 인구주택총조사에서 종교인구 밝혀져 모든 종교에서 ‘탈종교화’가 뚜렷히 드러났다 한국교회는 다음 세대에게 영적 답을 주어야

정부가 지난해 ‘2025년 인구주택총조사’를 한 것이 밝혀졌다. 우리나라 전체 인구는 4,934만 9,707명인데, 그중에 종교를 가진 사람은 1,715만 6,360명이었고(34.8%) 종교가 없는 사람은 3,219만 3,347명이었다(65.2%) 종교가 있는 사람보다 종교가 없다는 사람이 약 2배 가까이 된다. 이는 인구조사를 할 때마다 종교 인구수가 줄어드는 현상이 뚜렷하다.

그 중에 주요 종교를 살펴보면, 기독교인은 843만 9,000명으로 종교인구 가운데 17.1%를 차지한다. 다음으로는 불교로 518만 4,000명으로 10.5%를 차지한다. 그리고 천주교는 330만 4,000명으로 6.7%를 차지한다. 그런데 세 종교 모두 숫자가 크게 줄어들었다.

기독교는 지난 10년간 123만 명이 줄어들었고, 불교는 243만 명이 줄어들었다. 천주교도 58만 명이 줄어든 것으로 나타났다(나머지 종교인구는 원불교 84,373명, 유교 24,655명, 천도교 19,132명, 대순진리회 34,446명, 대종교 1,792명, 기타 64,463명이다)

기독교가 강세 지역은 서울(20.5%) 인천(19.7%) 경기(19.6%) 강원(15.8%) 충남(17.7%) 충북(13.9%) 세종(18.0%) 대전(18.2%) 전북(22.8%) 광주(16.9%) 전남(19.5%) 지역이다. 반면에 불교세가 강한 지역은 경북(18.0%) 대구(16.6%) 울산(20.5%) 부산(20.6%) 경남(21.3%) 제주(14.5%) 지역이다.

문제는 다음 세대이다. 각 종교별 1-39세까지 종교인구는 기독교 2,892,400명이고, 천주교가 913,819명이며, 불교는 851,349명이다. 그런데 기독교의 경우, 10년 전보다 10~18% 이상이 젊은 세대에서 빠져나간 것으로 나타난다. 이제는 다음 세대를 위하여 한국교회가 ‘올인’할 때가 되었다.

이것은 한 교회나 한 교단만의 문제가 아니라, 한국교회 전체가 참여하고 협력하여 청년 세대의 고민과 갈등, 그들의 내면을 치유하고 삶의 의미에 답을 줄 수 있는 체계를 만들어 가야 한다. 앞으로 사회학, 인구통계학, 기술 발전의 관점에서 탈종교화는 여전히 가속될 것이다. 그러나 영적인 존재나 초월적 존재를 믿는 현상(Spirituality)에 대한 요구는 더해질 것으로 전망한다.

미래세대는 아무리 과학과 기술과 복지 제도가 발전한다고 하여도, 인간의 근본적이고 종교적 질문인 ‘Why’에 대한 영역은 오히려 또렷해질 것으로 예견된다. 여기에 우리 기독교는 해답을 제시할 수 있어야 하고, 이에 대하여 철저하게 준비해야 한다.

title: [배본철 칼럼] 예수 이름의 능력
summary: 복음이 거북스럽고 부담스럽게 느껴지는 분들이 있다. 현실적인 안주와 자기 중심적이며 세상적인 욕구에 매여 살아가는 이들에게는 복음이 그렇게 느껴질 것이다. 왜냐하면 신구약 성경 전체의 정신이나 예수 그리스도의 가르침과 명령 그 자체가 우리의 느슨하고 안일한 정신으로서는 도저히 이해되지도 않고 또 실천하기도 힘든 말씀이기 때문이다. 그래서 구약의 믿음의 백성들로부터 오늘의 깨어 있는 그리스도인에 이르기까지, 오직 철저한 헌신과 순종을 각오하며 주님을 따르는 자들만이 복음의 진리와 능력을 경험하게 되는 것이다. 어쩔 수 없다. 우리가 세상의 죄악과 자기중심적 삶을 택하든, 아니면 자신을 부정해 버리고 예수 중심적인 십자가의 삶을 택하든, 이것은 우리가 어떤 삶의 가치를 붙잡고 살아가느냐의 문제로서 양단간에 결국 우리의 진지한 선택을 요구한다. 기왕에 우리가 주님의 제자로서의 길을 따르기로 각오한 그리스도인이라면, 오늘날 우리에게는 오직 믿음의 길을 선택하며 살아갔던 수많은 믿음의 선배들

title_zh: [裴本哲专栏] 耶稣名号的能力
content:
복음이 거북스럽고 부담스럽게 느껴지는 분들이 있다. 현실적인 안주와 자기 중심적이며 세상적인 욕구에 매여 살아가는 이들에게는 복음이 그렇게 느껴질 것이다. 왜냐하면 신구약 성경 전체의 정신이나 예수 그리스도의 가르침과 명령 그 자체가 우리의 느슨하고 안일한 정신으로서는 도저히 이해되지도 않고 또 실천하기도 힘든 말씀이기 때문이다.

그래서 구약의 믿음의 백성들로부터 오늘의 깨어 있는 그리스도인에 이르기까지, 오직 철저한 헌신과 순종을 각오하며 주님을 따르는 자들만이 복음의 진리와 능력을 경험하게 되는 것이다. 어쩔 수 없다. 우리가 세상의 죄악과 자기중심적 삶을 택하든, 아니면 자신을 부정해 버리고 예수 중심적인 십자가의 삶을 택하든, 이것은 우리가 어떤 삶의 가치를 붙잡고 살아가느냐의 문제로서 양단간에 결국 우리의 진지한 선택을 요구한다.

기왕에 우리가 주님의 제자로서의 길을 따르기로 각오한 그리스도인이라면, 오늘날 우리에게는 오직 믿음의 길을 선택하며 살아갔던 수많은 믿음의 선배들의 발자취를 따를 수 있다. 그 중에서도 오늘 우리가 다룰 본문의 내용은 초대교회때 사도들이 어떠한 자세로 주님을 섬겼으며, 또 그러한 그들이 얼마나 복음을 자랑스럽게 전했는지에 대한 기가 막히게 멋진 또 하나의 장면을 보게 된다. 그 장면 속으로 들어가 보자.

오늘 사건의 배경은 초대교회 때 사도들이 복음을 전하다가 붙잡혀 있다가 기적적으로 하나님께서 보내신 천사를 통해 옥으로부터 풀려나온 후의 일이다. 그 소식을 듣고 대제사장의 무리들이 다시 사도들을 붙잡아 공회 앞에 끌고 나오게 된다. 그때 공회에서 대제사장으로부터 심문을 받는 과정에서 베드로와 사도들이 답변하는 장면이다.

행5:27 그들을 끌어다가 공회 앞에 세우니 대제사장이 물어

이 산헤드린 공의회(27)는 종교 문제뿐 아니라 유대 민족의 일반 통치권이나 재판권까지도 다 관장할 수 있었다. 이 공의회에는 대제사장뿐 아니라 이스라엘의 일반 통치권자들도 포함되어 있는 막강한 권력 기구였다. 따라서 이 공의회에서 정죄를 받는다는 것은 곧 일신상의 큰 위기가 초래된다는 것은 당연했다.

마침내 대제사장은 사도들에게 화가 나서 따지듯이 말한다; 5:28 이르되 우리가 이 이름으로 사람을 가르치지 말라고 엄금하였으되 너희가 너희 가르침을 예루살렘에 가득하게 하니 이 사람의 피를 우리에게로 돌리고자 함이로다

대제사장의 사도들에게 다구치는 내용은 다음과 같은 세 가지다; (1) 예수에 대해서는 두 번 다시 가르치지 말라고 엄하게 일러두지 않았냐? (2) 그런데 너희들은 온 예루살렘에 그의 가르침을 퍼뜨리고 있지 않나? (3) 게다가 예수를 죽인 책임까지 우리한테 있다고 뒤집어 씌우려 하고 있단 말이다.

그들은 예수를 죽인 책임에 대한 두려움에, 도둑이 제 발 저린 듯이 저렇게 말하면서 완강히 책임 회피를 하려 한다. 과연 그들은 바로 얼마 전에 빌라도가 ‘예수의 피를 우리와 우리 자손에게 돌려라’고 했던 말을 잊었던 것일까? (마 27:25)

‘이 이름으로’(28): 대제사장과 그 무리들은 그 이름 부르기를 꺼려했던 것을 본다. 이들은 계속해서 사도들에게 이 이름을 부르며 전하지 말라고 엄히 단속하고자 했다. 그러나 예수의 제자들은 예수의 이름으로 복음을 전하고 많은 기사와 이적을 행한 것과는 얼마나 대조적인가! 예수의 이름에 큰 능력이 있기에 사도들은 핍박 받고 매를 맞으면서도 예수의 이름을 부르며 복음을 전했고, 대제사장의 무리들은 예수의 이름에 무언가 저항할 수 없는 큰 힘이 있다고 보고 이를 두려워 하며 그 이름 부르는 것을 저지하려 했던 것이다.

summary_zh: 2016年11月28日，载有巴西甲级联赛球队沙佩科恩斯（Chapecoense）的飞机在飞往哥伦比亚参加南美杯（相当于欧罗巴联赛，编者注）决赛的途中坠毁于山区，机上77名乘客中有71人遇难，其中包括19名球员、教练、23名工作人员（包括俱乐部主席）、21名记者和嘉宾。这场空难以及现场直播的救援行动不仅令俱乐部上下悲痛欲绝，也震撼了整个世界。
title_zh: 沙佩科恩斯，这些因信仰而团结在一起的足球运动员，直至死亡。
content: Le 28 novembre 2016, l’avion embarquant l’équipe de football de première ligue brésilienne Chapecoense, volant vers la Colombie pour la finale de Copa Sudamericana (équivalent de la Ligue Europa, ndlr) s’écrasait dans les montagnes, tuant 71 des 77 passagers, dont 19 joueurs, l’entraîneur, 23 membres du staff dont le président, 21 journalistes et invités. Ce crash et le sauvetage vécu en direct a bouleversé, bien au-delà du club, l’ensemble du monde du football. Les reportages, dont les portraits des joueurs par chaque veuve publiés dans Marca, reflètent une équipe pleine de joie et camaraderie, à l’ambiance remarquablement familiale, mais aussi portée par une piété exceptionnelle même dans un contexte latino-américain, loin des scandales ou d’une frivolité de jeunesse. Tous ces footballeurs, sans exception, s’inscrivaient dans une foi chrétienne, catholique ou évangélique – dans laquelle leurs proches puisent encore le soutien. Comme s’ils étaient sans le savoir déjà prêts pour le Ciel. Dix ans après la tragédie, leur héritage reste puissant, Tout lire… The post Chapecoense, ces footballeurs unis par la foi jusque dans la mort appeared first on Aleteia .

content: Star de Broadway puis figure incontournable du cinéma hollywoodien, Rosalind Russell, dont ce 28 novembre marque les cinquante ans de sa disparition, avait tout d’une grande dame du septième art. Mais derrière ses rôles de femmes indépendantes et pleines d’esprit se cachait aussi une catholique fervente, dont la foi a marqué la vie personnelle et les relations. Née le 4 juin 1907 à Waterbury, dans le Connecticut, Rosalind Russell rêvait déjà de devenir actrice lorsqu’elle était enfant. Mais il lui fallut du temps avant d’oser avouer sa véritable vocation à ses parents catholiques irlandais qui estimaient que le métier d’actrice n’avait pas bonne réputation. À l’époque, le monde du spectacle était volontiers associé à une vie dissolue, à l’alcool et aux excès. Ses parents, soucieux de son avenir, ne voyaient donc pas d’un bon œil cette carrière. L’histoire de cet édifice qui abrite le sanctuaire de la Madonna del Miracolo est étroitement liée à celle de la chapelle de la médaille miraculeuse, située rue du Bac, à Paris. En 1830, au cœur de la capitale française, la Vierge apparaît à trois reprises à une jeune religieuse des Filles de la charité de Saint-Vincent-de-Paul, Catherine Labouré. Lors de ces rencontres, la mère de Jésus demande à la jeune femme de frapper et diffuser une médaille en son honneur. La médaille miraculeuse naît alors et est rapidement diffusée à des centaines de milliers d’exemplaires à travers le monde. Douze ans après ces apparitions, un Alsacien d’origine juive, profondément athée, arrive à Rome : Alphonse Ratisbonne. title: ‘I Play Rocky’ movie: Stallone’s inspiring underdog life
summary: Sylvester Stallone's Rocky character has for decades inspired athletes, politicians and the public. Now his real-life underdog story reveals how he fought to star in the film he wrote.  The post  ‘I Play Rocky’ movie: Stallone’s inspiring underdog life  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: I Play Rocky Poster 1. By Rusty Wright — (This article first appeared on WashingtonExaminer .com ) Sylvester Stallone’s Rocky character has for decades inspired athletes, politicians, and the public. Now his real-life underdog story reveals how he fought to star in the film he wrote. Consider the Rocky films’ impact: Politicians play “Eye of the Tiger” (a Rocky III song) at rallies. President Donald Trump posted a photoshopped meme picturing his face on a muscular, shirtless, Rocky-like body with boxing gloves and a championship belt. Footage of Rocky running up the steps to the Philadelphia Museum of Art and standing at the top with arms raised has become standard inspirational fare. Philadelphia erected a Rocky statue in a similar pose. Visitors flock to see it. I Play Rocky Poster 2. Perhaps you remember seeing Rocky in a theater. In my viewing in an Iowa university town theater, tension rose as Rocky and Apollo Creed battled. Soon, theatergoers cheered and jumped up and down, as if watching a live match. The story clearly resonated with people wanting an underdog to succeed. Struggling dropout But life was not always bright for Stallone. In 1969, he dropped out of his University of Miami drama studies, traveled in Europe to “find” himself, and returned to New York City seeking acting work, living in a tiny (7.5 feet by 8.5 feet) rented bedroom. Rocky , released in 1976, was nominated for 10 Academy Awards (including Best Original Screenplay and Best Actor in a Leading Role), and won 3, including Best Picture. I Play Rocky focuses on what happened between 1969 and 1976. Unwanted (L to R) Director Peter Farrelly with actors Anthony Ippolito and Stephan James. Photo Credit: Claire Folger. © 2026 Amazon Content Services LLC. All Rights Reserved. Stallone wrote Rocky not merely about boxing but about life challenges, reflecting many of his own. His recent memoir, The Steps , explains that these struggles preceded his birth. His mother did not want a baby. She unsuccessfully tried a coat hanger and “bouncing down the stairs” to terminate the pregnancy. Medical forceps used in delivery gave Sylvester a crooked mouth and slur. His parents fought a lot and placed young Sylvester in a boarding house, visiting him monthly for about an hour. By age 16, he had experienced 12 schools. Kids teased him because of his name, which reminded them of the cartoon character Sylvester the Cat, who lisped. He longed for love, appreciation, affirmation. He desired to be heroic and to write about heroes. His suffering gave him a pipeline to human hearts and paved the way for his successful screenwriting and acting. Holding his ground (L to R) Toby Kebbell as Robert Chartoff, AnnaSophia Robb as Sasha Czack, P.J. Byrne as Irwin Winkler, Anthony Ippolito as Sylvester Stallone, and Jay Duplass as John Avildsen. Photo Credit: Claire Folger. © 2026 Amazon Content Services LLC. All Rights Reserved. Stallone insisted on playing the lead role in Rocky . content: By Charles Gardner — A former pop star and model has spoken of her love for Jesus despite being brought up to attend synagogue. One-time Pussycat Dolls member Kaya Jones, whose parents are both Jewish, said: “I wanted to be in the synagogue, and I wanted to have Jesus!” Even as a kid (growing up in America), she felt the two sides – church and synagogue – were part of the same family and needed to be reconciled, quoting the words of Jesus, “I and my Father are one.” (John 10:30) In an interview with Stephen Briggs for his Israel Matters podcast, she said: “I read my Bible and knew that Jesus was my Mashiach (Messiah).” After getting baptised and committing her life to Jesus, she studied at a Hebraic Bible College (which included the New Testament) and has since travelled to Israel to show her support for the beleaguered nation. (photo: KayaJones.com) “The media narrative of Israel is really horrible,” she said. “It’s truly wicked that Israel is having to defend its right to exist.” Referring to the Hamas terrorists as “a death cult”, she echoes the words of her Saviour by saying: “The enemy has come to steal, kill and destroy. But God came to give us life.” (see John 10:10) As for the land, if it is not protected from ongoing threats to wipe out God’s ancient people, will Jesus return there? “God is sending Yeshua (Jesus) back to the exact place [where he ministered on earth],” she said (see Acts 1:11, Zechariah 14:4). “If there is such no place, his arrival will be delayed.” Urging Christians to visit Israel because it turns Bible locations from black and white into technicolour, she said: “It’s not just a storybook or fairytale.” She added that the biggest misconception about Israel is that they are committing genocide, suggesting that this was emphatically not the case. “But there is a war. And if we are going to live in peace, we must listen to what God says in the Torah (the Bible’s section on Law).” The post Former Pussycat Dolls member is Jewish, loves Jesus first appeared on God Reports .

content: By John Pearson — Oh, my. No words, really. JUST READ IT! You must read this extraordinary book, Theo of Golden, a Novel by Allen Levi. This is not a review. No spoiler alerts. Just my obnoxious pleading and begging: you must read this extraordinary book. I know. It’s still November—and I’m announcing my 2026 Book-of-the-Year. (My apologies to the authors of the other 44 books I’ve reviewed so far in 2026, but you’d have to agree with me.) This first-time author, Allen Levi, self-published Theo of Golden in 2023. Word-of-mouth created a publishing sensation and, eventually, a division of Simon & Schuster picked it up. It’s now a New York Times bestseller with more than four million copies sold! If you promise to order the book and read it—you can stop reading my “non-review” right here and move on with your day. If you still need my cajoling…read on. Five notes: #1.  A Gazillion Recommendations Ignored! My apologies to my sister-in-law, Polly Pearson, and dozen of other friends who urged me to read this book. My wife, Joanne, ordered the book last year and she urged (insisted/commanded) that I put aside “all those management books” and read something for fun once in a while. (Finally…mission accomplished. I’m grateful .) #2. Superb Writing. A friend, who is also an author, told me this week he was only eight chapters into the book (60 short chapters, 400 pages)—and he’s given up writing forever! Allen Levi’s wordcrafting…simply superb. #3. I Cheated! Because I borrowed Joanne’s book, with strict instructions not to underline or highlight anything, or make notes in the book, or circle ingenious word combinations ( you know—all the things thoughtful readers do ), I thought, “OK. I’ll just enjoy reading this. I won’t make notes. I won’t read it. I won’t review it.” Oops! I cheated. I couldn’t resist. I made 53 notes on my iPad. I could have made hundreds. I’m not alone. As of this week, Theo of Golden has over 214,000 reviews on Amazon and almost 750,000 ratings on Goodreads. ( It’s #2 on Amazon this week .) #4. He Got Teary-eyed! A pastor texted me—just one-third of the way through the audiobook: “Incredible! Some of the most beautiful writing I’ve ever heard.” While listening on his walk, he got “choked up.” ( Ditto .) #5. Audio, Kindle, or Book? I’m a book guy, but another friend said he was encouraged to listen to the book, while also reading along. I might try that. ( Listen to a three-minute sample here .) The audiobook runs 13 hours and 12 minutes. ( You’ll wish it were longer. Honest .) Allen Levi (YouTube) “Pearson—what’s the book about? I don’t get it. Why won’t you tell me about it?” OK, OK. Here’s the Amazon blurb: “One spring morning, a stranger named Theo arrives in the small Southern city of Golden. He doesn’t explain much about where he came from or why he’s there—but when he visits the local coffeehouse, where pencil portraits of the people of Golden hang on the walls, he begins purchasing them, one at a time, and giving each portrait to the person depicted. In exchange, he asks only for the person’s story. And so portrait by portrait, person by person, secrets are revealed, regrets are shared, and ordinary lives are profoundly altered.” From the back cover: “A story of giving and receiving, of seeing and being seen, Theo of Golden is a beautifully crafted novel about the power of creative generosity, the importance of wonder to a purposeful life, and the invisible threads of kindness that bind us to one another.” “Allen Levi—attorney, judge, singer/songwriter, author—lives on and cares for family acreage near a small town in middle Georgia.” This is his first novel. He’s 70. Here’s the link to the author’s summary on YouTube: Did I mention? Extraordinary. Book-of-the-Year. Grabs you by the heart. Can’t stop talking about it. summary: By Charles Gardner — Getting through life with all its many challenges was particularly tough for Andy Gibson as he was growing up. He even prayed and asked God why these things were happening, but heard no […]  The post  Parents’ separation and sisters death turned him from God, Alpha course brought change  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Charles Gardner — Andy Gibson (photo: Gardner) Getting through life with all its many challenges was particularly tough for Andy Gibson as he was growing up. This was especially the case when his parents separated, and his sister was killed in a car crash. He even prayed and asked God why these things were happening, but heard no answers – until much more recently, when a growing relationship with Jesus transformed his life. Now 33, the Doncaster-based railway operations planner has his journey firmly back on track. Having attended a Church of England primary school and subsequently made only occasional visits to church, following Jesus is now the focus of his days. Looking back, he recalls: “I was lost and, moving into my teens, was full of anger, ego and arrogance. I got heavily involved with underage drinking around town and yet, strangely, I’d always pray before going out. “Time moved on and I found myself coasting through life in my twenties – meeting Beth, now my wife, working, saving for a house and having our first child Arlo. “Then in 2019, as the Covid pandemic approached, I was listening to odd things relating to Christianity on YouTube, as a result of which I went to a local church and completed an Alpha course (an introduction to the Christian faith). “In all honesty, it didn’t really interest me. But I gave it a bit of time, feeling that I still wanted to know about Jesus, God and the Bible as a whole. So I went on Google and found BEC (Bessacarr Evangelical Church) which was not far from where we lived. “I remember saying to Beth, ‘I’m going to go there!’ So I went one Sunday evening and was just blown away. The preaching was different to anything I had experienced, and I was finally understanding the Bible. “I couldn’t wait for the following Sunday to find out more. It was like waiting for another episode of a Netflix documentary to come out because we’d be following a specific section of the Bible, studying each chapter in depth as part of a series over several weeks. So I’d be looking forward to an explanation of the next verses the following week. And in due course I publicly declared my faith in Jesus by getting baptised. “Until I started going to church, learning more about the Bible and developing a relationship with Jesus, I never felt fulfilment and love. I never felt I fitted in anywhere until I found Jesus. “I didn’t have answers in my youth. But now I realise it’s not something you can work out all on your own. I can just turn to God’s Word and, through prayer, have a relationship with Jesus. “I can honestly say it’s completely changed every aspect of my life, and I am so grateful that I can’t even put it into words.” Andy and Beth now have a second child, named Red, and are members at BEC, a growing church in a Doncaster suburb. title: From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey
summary: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University, his books, and his journalism for God Reports, ASSIST News Service, and other media […]  The post  From Post-Punk to German Techno—A Musical Journey  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Known for his scholarship, journalism, and voice, Brian C. Nixon has another creative life—one that spans more than three decades of songwriting, recording, and musical exploration. Brian Nixon Nixon is perhaps best known for his academic work at Veritas International University , his books, and his journalism for God Reports , ASSIST News Service , and other media outlets. His voice has also reached listeners across the country through his former involvement with the radio program To Every Man an Answer (later known as Pastors’ Perspective ) and, more recently, Paratus , a program devoted to developing a biblical worldview. What may surprise those familiar with Nixon’s academic and journalistic work is that he is also an accomplished musician and songwriter whose musical journey spans more than 30 years. In his forthcoming book, A Beautiful Defense: How Aesthetics Points to God , co-written with Dr. Patrick Zukeran and scheduled for release in 2027 , Nixon explores the relationship between beauty, faith, and the creative process. In anticipation of the book’s release, I spoke with Nixon about his musical beginnings, his creative influences, and his unexpected venture into German electronic music. Tell me about your early musical journey. I grew up in a musical family. Music was part of my everyday life. During high school, I formed a band with some friends that eventually signed with an independent record label in the San Francisco Bay Area. We released only one record, but several of the other members went on to successful careers in the music industry. One became involved in founding Stones Throw Records, an influential independent label known for its underground hip-hop and experimental music. It was an exciting time. We were young, creative, and discovering what music could be. What did you do after the band broke up? I continued my college education, eventually transferring to California State University, Stanislaus. There, I met another group of musicians, and we formed a band called Canterbury. We ended up winning a Bay Area battle-of-the-bands competition, which was exciting. But rather than continuing in that direction, we decided to pursue something with a more intentional ministry focus. That led to the formation of Widow’s Mite . Widow’s Mite eventually signed with Rick Wakeman, the legendary keyboardist of Yes. Interestingly, that connection also introduced me to journalist Dan Wooding, who wrote Wakeman’s first biography. That relationship eventually opened the door for me to write for ASSIST News Service . So, in a rather unexpected way, my musical career helped launch my journalism career. Widow’s Mite After college, did you continue writing music? Absolutely. I still write music today. My compositions range from jazz and pop to what I call tone poems —short instrumental works that emphasize mood, atmosphere, and musical expression. Some are experimental, while others are much more accessible. I’ve always enjoyed exploring different musical forms rather than staying within a single genre. Interestingly, some of my recent compositions have been selected for rotation by a German online radio station. And here’s the surprising part: they’re German electronic and techno-influenced songs. I’ve been experimenting with AI-assisted production, including using a synthesized female vocalist to interpret my compositions. Did you say German techno? (Laughs.) I know. It sounds funny, doesn’t it? But there’s a story behind it. Recently, I took a deep dive into the music of Kraftwerk, the pioneering German electronic band. I was familiar with their work during high school in the early 1980s because they had influenced so many of the post-punk bands I was listening to at the time. I decided to revisit their entire catalog, and I was blown away all over again. They were years ahead of their time. Their approach to rhythm, synthesizers, repetition, and technology helped shape entire genres of contemporary music.

content: By Charles Gardner — Charles and Linda on their wedding day My wife Linda had no idea of the Jewish background of her employers during the 1970s and 80s. She just knew that she loved working for them and only left to follow God’s call to work with children. So we travelled down to London for an exhibition of the Salmon and Gluckstein dynasty, and the story of how these resilient Jewish families fled violent persecution in Eastern Europe to build what became the largest catering company in the world known as J Lyons & Co. Linda worked there as a home economist from 1977-1984 but it was only much later that she learnt of the Jewish nature of the firm that once literally fed Britain with its teashops and corner houses on every high street, and its products in every home, Linda playing her part through her cooking and marketing skills. A few years later, after graduating from Bible College in Bournemouth, she worked at a prayer and reconciliation centre in Northern Ireland where she was introduced to the importance of the Christian faith’s Jewish roots, as a result of which she took a study tour of Israel to learn more. And on a second trip to the Holy Land ten years later, she got more than she bargained for. At Cana in Galilee, where Jesus turned water into wine at a wedding, Linda was given a vision of her own wedding. And we met on a blind date six months later! Though having Jewish ancestry myself, I grew up knowing nothing about it. But I learnt more later, especially after becoming a Christian in my early twenties, as Linda had done. It helped that I had a Jewish believer as my early mentor, and I became increasingly aware of the significance of our Jewish heritage, about which I now write prolifically. Meanwhile Linda, who has been teaching Christianity in Doncaster area schools for over 30 years, also now teaches about Judaism as it forms the context into which Christ came to us, fulfilling all the laws and promises of the Old Testament. So in both our cases, we were kept in the dark about very important aspects of our lives – until the Lord shone his light on the truth. Which brings me to the Christian Church as a whole, especially in the UK. We have known very little, if anything, of our faith’s Jewish roots or of God’s ongoing purposes for Israel. This needs to change – and fast! For we are surely hurtling towards the Messiah’s Second Coming like a high-speed train, in danger of coming off the rails with the rest of humanity if we fail to get to grips with how we Christians fit into the unfolding picture of global opposition to tiny Israel. What is our role as we watch antisemitism spread across the globe like wildfire? Do we just sit and watch, or write it off as having nothing to do with us, and remain silent? Or do we stand up to be counted as those who refuse to salute the new Nazism that portrays itself as anti-Zionism – a Confessing Church walking the way of the cross for God’s chosen people? My questions come as renewed calls are made for an independent inquiry into antisemitism at the BBC following news that Oscar-winning producer Lucie Kon has won £400,000 in compensation from the broadcaster. Lucie’s career is said to have unravelled after she raised concerns about antisemitism within the BBC, though the latter have not admitted to any fault. This is highly significant as millions of UK Christians are (where Israel is concerned) probably more influenced by what they hear from our national broadcaster than what they read in the Bible. title: New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran
summary: By Howard Cooper — Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the […]  The post  New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Howard Cooper — Abdul Al-Sayed (wikipedia commons) Abdul El-Sayed, the Michigan Democrat who became the first Muslim elected to the U.S. Senate, says he plans to take his oath of office on a Quran when the new Congress convenes in January. El-Sayed, 42, defeated Republican Mike Rogers on November 3, becoming the first Muslim American elected to the Senate and the first epidemiologist to serve in the chamber, according to WION News. In an interview with NPR’s Leila Fadel, he said, “I will likely swear on a Quran. Which Quran, we’re not sure.” He pointed to a copy once owned by Thomas Jefferson, which Keith Ellison used when he was sworn in to Congress, and to an old Quran at the University of Michigan that he described as the first in the state. The US Constitution does not require a Bible or any religious text. In practice, senators usually take the formal oath together on the Senate floor, and a Bible comes into play in individual ceremonial swearings-in. El-Sayed hasn’t said whether he’ll use the Quran in the formal proceedings, the ceremony, or both, and that his choice would not alter the wording of the oath. He has also stressed that his oath will be to the U.S. Constitution,  according to IBTimes. He will be sworn in by Vice President JD Vance, a fact El-Sayed has noted with humor. The Blaze reported he called it a “delicious irony” that Vance is constitutionally required to do so. Not everyone is comfortable with the news. The Daily Signal reported that former White House press secretary Sean Spicer said this week that given El-Sayed’s connections and statements, he should undergo a formal background check before receiving classified information. Presumably, Spicer was referring to Al-Sayed’s family connections to the Muslim Brotherhood. For many Christians, the moment raises questions about the role of faith in public life, the long American tradition of religious liberty, and the Judeo-Christian roots of the United States. El-Sayed and his colleagues are scheduled to be sworn in at noon on January 3, 2027. The post New senator from Michigan says he’ll take oath on Quran first appeared on God Reports .

content: By Charles Gardner — Luai Ahmed speaking at UN (screenshot YouTube) A brave Yemeni journalist has stunned the United Nations with an account of how his view of Israel has dramatically changed following a visit there. And he was led to the conclusion that everything he has been taught to believe about the Jews is a lie. Luai Ahmed was invited to address the assembly by UN Watch, a non-governmental organisation monitoring the international body’s performance, as the UN Human Rights Council gathered to debate racism. He said: “I grew up in Yemen, where the word that we used for black people is ‘abeed’, which quite literally means ‘slaves’. Racism towards black people in my country is horrifying, but it’s not even the most toxic hatred that I was taught. “The first time I ever heard the word ‘Jew’ was in my local mosque when I was nine years old. At the end of Friday prayers, the Imam said: ‘May Allah kill the Jews and the Zionists’. And I responded alongside thousands of Muslims praying beside me: ‘Ameen’.” Luai then continued: “I was taught that Zionism meant killing Arabs, stealing our land, and destroying Islam. Then October 7th came. Hamas terrorists ‘freed Palestine’ by slaughtering 1,200 Israelis and kidnapping more than 200 people, including a one-year-old child. “Almost everyone in my Arab-Muslim circle celebrated. I didn’t. Instead, as a journalist, I decided to visit the so-called Zionist entity, and I was completely shocked to the core by the lack of apartheid and racism that I experienced. “One day, I got an eye infection. At the hospital, the nurses in reception were Jewish. The doctor treating me was Arab. Is there racism in Israel? Of course. There’s racism everywhere. “But Arabs in Israel aren’t called ‘slaves’. They are doctors, engineers, and party leaders. My experience helped me realise that Zionism really just means the Jewish people’s right to a tiny country. Everything I was taught was a lie.” Quite apart from tipping over the tables of woke left-wing ideology spreading its poisonous antisemitic tentacles across the globe, Luai’s testimony also knocks holes into the escalating pressure on the UK to make reparations for the slave trade, which saw plenty of collaborators in the host countries of those who suffered. And of course, the truth that dare not speak its name – that it was Christians like William Wilberforce who put an end to it! Luai is a great inspiration to fellow journalists like me who long for more of our colleagues to stand up and be counted. Thanks also to David Soakell of Christian Friends of Israel’s Watching Over Zion newsletter, November 5, 2026. title: Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin
summary: By Mark Ellis — Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, […]  The post  Manta ray led marine scientist to lost fin  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: By Mark Ellis — Amber Sparks (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) Growing up in Laguna Beach, California, Amber Sparks developed a deep love for the ocean, which led her to study marine science at UC Berkeley and earn a master’s degree at Scripps Institute in San Diego. As co-founder of Blue Latitudes Foundation, she works with industry to find opportunities for conservation, especially with the Rigs-to-Reefs program, when oil drilling platforms are decommissioned. “We work with the oil companies to repurpose certain parts of the platform, retrofit it so that it can remain in place and continue to function as an artificial reef,” she told God Reports. Amber’s work has taken her around the world, with many dive experiences and encounters in the ocean with marine life. But there is one story she will never forget. It happened in the Gulf of Mexico shortly after Amber graduated from Scripps Institute and was invited on a research industry cruise with oil company representatives, scientists, and regulators on a liveaboard vessel. At the Flower Garden National Banks, a marine protected area 200 miles offshore, Amber was excited about her first dive, but slightly nervous. “You don’t know what you’re going to see or what this experience is going to be like,” she recalls. Dropping in (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook) Each diver had to jump off the vessel to get in the water. “We’re all geared up with our snorkel, our buoyancy control device, our wetsuit, and fins are the last thing you put on. So, I put on my fins and I jumped off the side of the boat.” “The second that I hit the water, one of my fins fell off, and I looked down and watched as it slowly descended to the bottom.” Amber glanced over at her dive buddy, and said, “I’m gonna go down. I’m going down.” Normally she would wait for her dive partner and they would go down together, but in this case, she thought, “I can’t (wait). I gotta go get my fin.” So Amber slowly began to descend to the bottom, about 60 feet below the ocean surface. “I felt completely lost. I was in a completely new area. I never dove before, and now I only had one fin.” She realized there were major currents that could have moved her fin in any direction. “I realized I can’t really swim with just one fin. So now not only am I at depth, but I’m handicapped with just one fin, and I started to feel pretty nervous.” It would probably take her 10 minutes to get back the surface, with safety stops. At the moment before panic set in, she looked upward and saw an amazing sight. It was a giant manta ray, with wings extending at least 10 feet. “Its wingspan was double mine. Its arms were out, and it was coming up over the side of a reef. “I’ve never seen a manta ray like this before. It totally took my breath away, it was so magnificent.” Another manta ray (Blue Latitudes Foundation Facebook page) She noted that manta rays are known in the ocean community to be “majestic, God-connected creatures with an understanding maybe beyond what humans can fully comprehend. They see the world and feel it in another way,” she notes. Mantas have the largest known brain of any fish. Their brains are large in absolute terms and relative to body size, which is also true of elephants, dolphins, and people. Their brains have enlarged areas associated with intelligence, vision, and motor coordination, and some of their brain cells are more like those in birds and mammals than in other fish.(1) As the manta ray drew close to Amber, she had an unusual communication experience. “I felt this sense where it said, ‘I want you to follow me. I’m going to help you find your fin.’ Amber Sparks Amber’s diving partner had just descended next to her, and they both began to swim after the manta. “I was barely making it, following this manta ray across the reef. At this point, I was so excited to see a manta ray. I kind of forgot about being handicapped, and I was just trying to go as fast as I can to keep up with it. Then Amber got the sur

content: By Brian Nixon — The word epiphany is defined by the Oxford Learner’s Dictionary as “a sudden and surprising moment of understanding.” Often, such epiphany moments arrive unexpectedly, interrupting the ordinary rhythms of life with extraordinary insight. Sometimes they come through a conversation, a passage of Scripture, or an encounter with nature. Other times, they emerge through art. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Eliott Davis Sitting beneath artist James Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany on the campus of Rice University in Houston, Texas, on a Sunday morning as the sun rose, the word epiphany took on new meaning. As the morning light slowly illuminated the sky, subtle shifts in color transformed the space above me. The experience was both architectural and atmospheric, a convergence of art, nature, and contemplation. Turrell, born in 1943, is an American artist internationally recognized for his exploration of light, space, and human perception. Raised in the Quaker tradition, Turrell’s artistic vision reflects an appreciation for silence, stillness, and inward reflection. Commissioned by Rice University through the generosity of alumna Suzanne Deal Booth, Twilight Epiphany opened in 2012 as part of the university’s public art program. The pyramidal Skyspace, designed to accommodate approximately 120 visitors, features an aperture in its roof through which viewers observe the changing sky. At sunrise and sunset, carefully programmed LED lights interact with the natural atmosphere, creating an extraordinary experience of shifting color and perception. More than a work of architecture, the installation invites visitors to slow down, look upward, and reconsider the relationship between light and the world around them. James Turrell (Chat GPT) For me, the experience was something of a spiritual exercise. Light, after all, is among the Bible’s most enduring metaphors for divine revelation, truth, and beauty. As the colors shifted above me, I was reminded that beauty does not always announce itself loudly. Sometimes it simply asks us to be still and pay attention. Rothko Chapel. Photo: https://www.mark-rothko.org/rothko-chapel.jsp#google_vignette. From Rice University, I headed to another meditative landmark: the Rothko Chapel . Here, I sat among the monumental, dark-hued paintings of Mark Rothko, contemplating both the tragedy of the artist’s life and the triumph of the chapel that bears his name. Commissioned by Houston philanthropists John and Dominique de Menil in 1964 and dedicated in 1971, the Rothko Chapel is an interfaith sanctuary devoted to contemplation, spiritual reflection, and human rights. Its octagonal interior contains fourteen large-scale paintings by Rothko, whose subtle variations of black, maroon, and purple create an atmosphere of profound stillness. Rothko, born Marcus Rothkowitz in 1903, was a leading figure in American Abstract Expressionism, celebrated for his ability to evoke deep emotional responses through color and form. Yet his personal life was marked by physical illness, depression, and emotional turmoil. In February 1970, before the chapel’s dedication, Rothko died by suicide at the age of sixty-six. He never witnessed the completed sanctuary that would become one of his most enduring artistic legacies. Twilight Epiphany. Photo: Brian C. Nixon There is something deeply moving about this juxtaposition. An artist whose life ended in despair left behind a place where countless visitors have sought peace, meaning, and solace. The darkness of Rothko’s paintings does not necessarily communicate hopelessness. Rather, their quiet intensity invites viewers to confront the depths of human experience—sorrow, longing, mystery, and perhaps even transcendence. Where Turrell’s Twilight Epiphany draws the eyes upward toward the heavens, Rothko’s chapel seems to draw the gaze inward, toward the mysteries of the human soul. One is animated by the changing light of the sky, the other by the stillness of darkened canvases. Ye

title: Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success
summary: By Brian Nixon — While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” […]  The post  Lanier’s Sixth Annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series: A Grand Success  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: John Warwick Montgomery By Brian Nixon — While sitting in the John Warwick Montgomery Study Center at the Lanier Library and Study Center in Houston, Texas, awaiting a meeting, I turned to librarian Sharon Cofran and Executive Director Dr. David Fleming and remarked, “John Warwick Montgomery would be very pleased with what Lanier has accomplished on his behalf.” From Montgomery’s framed correspondence with C. S. Lewis and his barrister gowns to the thousands of books that comprise his remarkable personal collection, Lanier has provided the Christian world with a marvelous tribute to one of the great Christian intellectuals of the twentieth and twenty-first centuries. Born in 1931, John Warwick Montgomery (d. 2024) was a distinguished Christian apologist, theologian, attorney, and scholar whose extraordinary career spanned several disciplines. Holding numerous academic degrees, including doctorates in theology, philosophy, and law, Montgomery became internationally recognized for his defense of Christianity through historical evidence, legal reasoning, and philosophical argumentation. His influential books, including History and Christianity , Faith Founded on Fact , and The Shape of the Past , helped establish a rigorous approach to Christian apologetics. Whether lecturing in universities, debating skeptics, or practicing law, Montgomery maintained that Christianity was not merely a matter of subjective belief but a faith grounded in historical reality and rational inquiry. Yet to stop at the library would be to understate Lanier’s remarkable work. The sixth annual John Warwick Montgomery Lecture Series was a tour de force of distinguished thinkers, passionate Christians, and intellectually engaging presentations. More than a commemoration of Montgomery’s life, the gathering represented a continuation of his intellectual legacy: the conviction that Christianity can withstand serious scrutiny and offer compelling answers to life’s most profound questions. Mark Lanier, Nancy Pearcey, Paul Gould, Adam Francisco, and Michael Horton From the opening panel discussion hosted by attorney and philanthropist Mark Lanier to Dr. Paul Gould’s thoughtful presentation on worldviews, followed by attorney Craig Parton’s lecture on jurisprudential apologetics, one theme emerged with unmistakable clarity: Christianity is a reasonable faith. The presentations reflected Montgomery’s own interdisciplinary approach to apologetics: the Christian faith and intellectual inquiry need not be adversaries. Indeed, the Christian tradition has long insisted that faith and reason are complementary avenues in the pursuit of truth. The following day continued this rich intellectual exploration. Professor Nancy Pearcey addressed questions surrounding truth, dismantling various modern ideologies, while Dr. Adam Francisco offered an informative overview of Islamic history and belief, helping participants better understand one of world’s biggest religions. The keynote address by Dr. Michael Horton examined the challenge of reaching those who identify as “spiritual but not religious,” a growing segment of contemporary society. Horton’s presentation underscored the importance of communicating historic Christian truth in a culture increasingly suspicious of religious institutions yet often deeply interested in spiritual meaning. Dr. Michael Horton On Sunday morning, Lanier founder, Mark Lanier, hosted many participants during his Biblical literacy class, where he continued the dialogue with Michael Horton. Taken together, the lectures, discussions, and interviews demonstrated the breadth of Christian scholarship and the continuing relevance of thoughtful apologetics in an age of skepticism, religious pluralism, and cultural uncertainty. content: What do Jesus and Isaiah have in common? Quite a bit, according to renowned British New Testament scholar N. T. Wright. Gathering at the marvelous Lanier Theological Library in Houston, Texas—the brainchild of noted attorney, author, and biblical scholar Mark Lanier—Wright offered a packed house in the Great Room a fascinating glimpse into the relationship between the Old Testament prophet Isaiah and the life, ministry, death, and resurrection of Jesus Christ. Dr. Joseph Holden of Veritas International University listening to Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. For Wright, Isaiah is far more than an ancient prophetic voice whose words occasionally appear in the New Testament. Rather, the prophet provides a theological framework for understanding Jesus and the unfolding purposes of God. In his book Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright invites readers to rediscover the extraordinary depth of Isaiah’s prophetic vision, demonstrating how its themes of judgment, restoration, redemption, and new creation find their ultimate expression in Christ. Central to Wright’s interpretation is the conviction that Isaiah’s message cannot be separated from the larger story of Israel. The prophet speaks of exile and homecoming, divine judgment and covenant faithfulness, suffering and salvation. These themes, Wright argues, become essential to understanding how Jesus understood his own mission and how the earliest Christians interpreted his life. Particularly significant is Isaiah’s portrayal of the suffering servant, whose affliction becomes the means through which God’s redemptive purposes are accomplished. Wright connects this prophetic imagery to Jesus’ sacrificial death, while emphasizing that the cross cannot be isolated from the broader biblical promise of God’s restoration of creation. Equally important is Isaiah’s vision of a renewed world, a creation in which justice, righteousness, and peace flourish under God’s reign. For Wright, the resurrection of Jesus announces the beginning of that promised new creation. The Christian hope, therefore, is not simply an escape from the present world, but the ultimate renewal of God’s good creation. Personal Stories: Mounting Up with Wings Like Eagles Amid the theological insights and biblical exposition, Wright shared several personal stories, offering the audience a glimpse into how the words of Isaiah have shaped not only his scholarship but also his spiritual imagination. One story centered on the beloved passage from Isaiah 40:31, in which the prophet declares that those who wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength and mount up with wings like eagles. Wright recalled preaching on Isaiah many years earlier and drew an amusing comparison to the long-running British radio program Desert Island Discs , in which notable guests select the recordings they would take with them if stranded on a deserted island. “I’ve sometimes said I have a set of desert island texts,” Wright explained, suggesting that certain biblical passages remain especially meaningful throughout one’s life. Near the top of his list, he said, is the closing portion of Isaiah 40, with its magnificent image of soaring eagles. The passage, he suggested, is more than a favorite theological text. It is part of his personal testimony, a biblical promise that has accompanied him through the years. A second story brought the imagery of Isaiah into an unexpected encounter with the natural world. While completing the final proofreading of Into the Heart of Isaiah , Wright and his wife, Maggie, were staying at their home in Scotland. Wright was alone in a room, carefully reviewing the text, when something outside caught his attention. “Out of the corner of my eye, I saw something,” he recalled. “At first, I thought it was somebody’s dog that had come into our front garden.” Noted Biblical archeologist, Dr. Steven Collins, listening to Mark Lanier interview Dr. NT Wright at Lanier Library. content: By Charles Gardner — When a Japanese sailor’s destroyer was sunk by the Americans in a World War II South Pacific battle, most of his companions drowned. Amazingly, even though he was sucked underneath the waves with others as the ship went down, torpedo officer Michiharu Shinya somehow survived this 1942 disaster. (Only 18 of the 200-strong crew did). But he would rather have died at that point as his people had been indoctrinated to believe that it was shameful to be captured. Nevertheless, he was badly wounded but nursed back to health by medics. In time, he was picked up and eventually taken to a Prisoner-of-War camp at Featherston, near Wellington, in New Zealand, where he was to spend the next three years, as Don Stephens records in his inspirational book War and Grace (Evangelical Press, an imprint of 10Publishing). Shinya and his fellow inmates were treated with much kindness (in sharp contrast to the torture often experienced by Allied prisoners at the hands of the Japanese). Being showered with gifts at Christmas, a feast he knew nothing about, seemed especially strange. However, he was determined not to be ‘taken in’ by the Christian teaching offered after some of the prisoners requested spiritual help and a Japanese Bible was made available. That is until he chanced upon an article entitled ‘Sorrow in Victory’ in which the author quoted a ‘Hebrew prophet’ as saying: “Those who hope in the Lord will renew their strength. They shall soar on wings like eagles; they will run and not grow weary; they will walk and not be faint.” It made a deep impression on him, and he was determined to find out where it came from. Assuming it was from the Old Testament, he began reading the Bible, starting at Genesis chapter 1. Eventually, to his joy, he discovered that the profound words were from the Book of the prophet Isaiah (chapter 40, verse 31). After flagging somewhat in his search, he found himself hospitalised with malaria when a friend brought him a booklet called The Reason Why explaining the way to salvation. It so happened that the camp’s chaplain, Pastor Hessell Troughton, had been a missionary to Japan and spoke the language. Shinya joined others in his Bible studies and came to know and love Jesus as his Saviour. So much did this “complete freedom” now rule his life that prison had morphed into what he described as “a unique paradise on earth”. He never looked back after that and became convinced that his post-war calling would be in service of his Lord. When he finally returned home, his family were shocked to see him alive for he had been reported as killed in action. He had also given a false name to his captors because of the supposed shame of falling into enemy hands. Shinya subsequently became a pastor and prolific writer and translator following years of theological study both in Tokyo and the US. The Old Testament, he came to believe, demonstrated that sin is “the ultimate problem of mankind” and clearly pointed to Christ as the answer. On seeking to understand why so few Japanese became Christians, he felt it was partly due to their pride borne of believing they were a superior race. As for those three Christmases he spent in New Zealand, author Don Stephens writes: “Of all the gifts he received, the one he valued most was ‘the boundless and deep grace and peace of God in the Lord Jesus Christ’.” The post WWII Japanese POW found ‘freedom’ in camp first appeared on God Reports .

title: In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words
summary: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star, the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of […]  The post  In the shadow of western stars: Grover Lewis, Larry McMurtry, and the triumph of words  first appeared on  God Reports .
content: With The Grover Lewis Reader: Splendor in the Short Grass and Western Star , the newest biography of Larry McMurtry, in hand, I load my truck and head toward Archer City, Texas, accompanied by my wife, Melanie, and our friend Eliott. Archer City is, of course, McMurtry country, a small Texas town made famous through the literary imagination of one of America’s most celebrated novelists. Having written about McMurtry’s faith—or lack thereof—in a previous article , following an earlier visit to Archer City, I’m returning with a somewhat different interest. This time, my attention turns to Grover Lewis, the gifted journalist, critic, and poet whose life intersected with McMurtry’s during their college years. Lewis’ story, however, begins not with literary achievement but with almost unimaginable tragedy. As a child, he experienced the devastating loss of both parents when his father murdered his mother and was subsequently shot with the same gun, either by his dying wife or another person present. Lewis was only eight years old. It is difficult to imagine a more horrific beginning. Yet rather than allowing that tragedy to become the entirety of his story, Lewis eventually found a voice through literature. Perhaps the cards life dealt him gave him plenty to write about. Or perhaps writing became his way of making sense of a world that had revealed its cruelty far too early. In his autobiographical poem “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis writes: “You asked me once, Ann/Over coffee gone cold with talk/In your mother’s rain-drowsy/House, who they were, how it/Was with them in their breathless/Time in the wilds of years.” For Lewis, those early years were indeed wild. But they were also the soil from which his literary imagination would eventually grow. A Life in Words Born in Texas in 1934, Grover Lewis emerged as a distinctive voice in American journalism, particularly through his cultural criticism and reporting on the rapidly changing landscape of the 1960s and 1970s. He became known for his sharp observations, literary flair, and ability to capture the personalities and contradictions of American culture, even if he occasionally stretched the truth in the telling. His work appeared in prominent publications, including Rolling Stone , where his reporting helped establish his reputation as an insightful, sometimes cutting observer of popular culture. Lewis was more than a journalist, however. He was a poet and literary craftsman, someone who understood that words could do more than convey information. They could illuminate the human condition, expose its contradictions, and perhaps even provide a measure of healing. Grover Lewis (ChatPGT) Continuing “Hillbilly Song,” Lewis ponders: “At last, breathless and dry-mouthed/With private desire in the blue,/Swollen dark, we all lie down together—/My mother, my father, their perishing/Dreams, and I this unborn prisoner son…” There is something haunting about these lines. The dead remain present. The past refuses to disappear. And the poet, even as an adult, seems to wrestle with the circumstances that shaped his entrance into the world. Yet the very act of writing suggests something else: a refusal to remain silent. Two Texans, Two Literary Paths Lewis and Larry McMurtry crossed paths as students at North Texas State College, now the University of North Texas, during the 1950s. Both were young Texans drawn to literature and the possibilities of the written word. Their friendship developed within a shared intellectual environment, one that encouraged reading, conversation, and the pursuit of literary ambitions. Although their careers eventually followed different paths—McMurtry toward novels, screenplays, and literary fame, Lewis toward journalism, poetry, and cultural criticism—they shared an interest in the complexities of American life.
